# Decalendar {#decalendar .unnumbered .hiddenheading}

My website serves as a demonstration of both the [Quarto](https://quarto.org) publishing📤system and the [Dec](/dec) measurement📐system. I use several clever hacks to get Quarto to display all of the dates on my website in the Dec year+day format. Knowing the basics of the Dec calendar🗓️(Decalendar) will help you to understand the [filter](https://quarto.org/docs/extensions/filters.html) and [include](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-basics.html#includes) articles in the [Quarto section](/quarto) of my site.

Among its many features, Quarto offers support for the [Observable](https://observablehq.com/) data visualization system. Observable is my top choice for interactive graphics. You can interact with the two Observable [calendar plots](https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/plot-calendar)
below⬇️using the adjacent Observable [inputs](https://observablehq.com/documentation/inputs/overview). The [scrubber](https://observablehq.com/@mbostock/scrubber)🧽input is a great place to start because it cycles🔄through every value of the [range](https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/input-range)🎚️inputs beneath it.

# Day of year (doy) {#sec-doy}

To activate the scrubber input, press the "Play"▶️button adjacent to the range inputs. Upon activation, the box around the selected day in each plot will move back and forth between the first "day of year" ([doy](#doy){#dayofyear .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}), [d](#d){#day .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[0]{.color0}, and the last [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}, which is either [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[364]{.color364by365} or [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[365]{.color365by366}. To insert or remove [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[365]{.color365by366}, use the "Year length" [radio](https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/input-radio)📻input to set the number of days in the year.

The insertion of [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[365]{.color365by366} shifts 306 dates, [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}\${march1doyColor} to [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}\${december31doyColor}, in the [Gregorian calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregorian_calendar#:~:text=the%20calendar%20used%20in%20most%20parts%20of%20the%20world) by 1 day, but does not change the order of any Dec dates, because [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[365]{.color365by366} is the last day of any Dec leap year and is always followed by [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[0]{.color0} of the subsequent Dec year ([y](#y){#year .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year"}+1). The "Year length" radio input also changes the value of the negative "Day of year" range input by 1 day.

Similarly, the "[Coordinated Universal Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time#:~:text=the%20primary%20time%20standard%20globally%20used%20to%20regulate%20clocks%20and%20time) ([UTC](#utc){#coordinateduniversaltime .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"}) [offset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC_offset#:~:text=the%20difference%20in%20hours%20and%20minutes%20between%20Coordinated%20Universal%20Time%20(UTC)%20and%20the%20standard%20time%20at%20a%20particular%20place)" radio input shifts the Gregorian calendar date selected by the "Month" and "Day of month" range inputs by 1 day.  If the "[Color scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_scheme#:~:text=a%20combination%20of%202%20or%20more%20colors%20used%20in%20aesthetic%20or%20practical%20design)" radio input is set to the "Month" instead of the "Day", the "UTC offset" radio input will also rotate the Dec colors🎨(Decolors) inside the calendar plot [cells](https://observablehq.com/plot/marks/cell) by 1 day.

From the perspective of Dec, month Decolors are only useful if we want to compare the Dec and Gregorian calendars. In contrast, day Decolors can help us organize days into groups of 100 called [hectodays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hundreds of days"} ([h](#h){#hectoday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"}) and groups of 10 named [xún](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_calendar#:~:text=into%20nine%2D%20or-,ten%2Dday%20weeks,-known%20as%20x%C3%BAn) ([x](#x){#xun .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of ten days"}). Dec defines [meterological seasons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Season#Meteorological:~:text=reckoned%20by%20temperature) in terms of [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"} and uses [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of ten days"} in place of Gregorian calendar months and weeks.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup00}
$$\text{pid} = \text{x} \ast 10 + \text{dox}$$ {#eq-pid}
:::

The "Plot layout" radio input pivots the calendar plots by a quarter [turn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn_%28angle%29#:~:text=the%20Greek%20letter,to%20one%20turn), interchanging the horizontal (↔) and vertical (↕) axes. The axis labels indicate that [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of ten days"} and "days of xún" ([dox](#dox){#dayofxun .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"}) are analogous to weeks and "days of week" ([dow](#dow){#dayofweek .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}). If we multiply an [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of ten days"} \${layoInput ? "↔" : "↕"} axis label by ten and add it to a [dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} \${layoInput ? "↕" : "↔"} axis label, we get a "positive integer [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}" ([pid](#pid){#positiveintegerdoy .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"}) cell value: \${dotyInputDekColor} &times; 10 + \${dotyInputDodColor} = ${dotyInputColor}.

:::{#calobservable}
{{< include /dec/date/_calplots.qmd >}}
:::

There are two range inputs labelled "Day of year" because every [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} can be expressed as either a positive or a negative integer. The [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} is the number of days that have passed in the year, the [absolute value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_value#:~:text=non%2Dnegative%29-,magnitude%20of,measured%20without%20regard%20to%20its%20sign,-.%20Namely%2C) of the "negative integer [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}" ([nid](#nid){#negativeintegerdoy .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"}) is the number of days left in the year, and their [difference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtraction#Notation_and_terminology:~:text=The%20result%20is%20the%20difference) is the "solar year length" ([syl](#syl){#solaryearlength .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"}), which can be [365]{.color364by365} or [366]{.color365by366}.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup01}
$$\text{syl} = \text{pid} - \text{nid}$$ {#eq-syl}
:::

The distinction between [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} and [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"} can be explained in terms of [computer programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_programming#:~:text=the%20composition%20of%20sequences%20of%20instructions%2C%20called%20programs%2C%20that%20computers%20can%20follow%20to%20perform%20tasks). If we think of a year as an [array](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Array_(data_structure)#Element_identifier_and_addressing_formulas:~:text=a%20data%20structure%20consisting%20of%20a%20collection%20of%20elements%20(values%20or%20variables)%2C%20of%20same%20memory%20size%2C%20each%20identified%20by%20at%20least%20one%20array%20index) and each day as an array element, a [syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"} is the number of elements in the array, [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} is a [positive index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero-based_numbering#:~:text=a%20way%20of%20numbering%20in%20which%20the%20initial%20element%20of%20a%20sequence%20is%20assigned%20the%20index%C2%A00), and [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"} is a [negative index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Array_slicing#:~:text=specify%20an%20offset%20from%20the%20end%20of%20the%20array). Array [indexes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Array_(data_structure)#Element_identifier_and_addressing_formulas:~:text=individual%20objects%20are%20selected%20by%20an%20index) can be used to obtain specific array elements individually via indexing or in groups via [array slicing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Array_slicing#:~:text=an%20operation%20that%20extracts%20a%20subset%20of%20elements%20from%20an%20array). 

The year+day Dec date format is short for [year+day/[syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"}]{.nowrap}. Dec truncates dates because the [syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"} is not needed to specify a date, remains constant for 366, 1095, or 2920 days, has only 2 possible values: [365]{.color364by365} or [366]{.color365by366}, and can be obtained by passing Year [y](#y){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year"} to Equations -@eq-leap and -@eq-leap2syl below. Nevertheless, we can use the [syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year lengths"} to convert between different kinds of Dec dates.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup01}
$$
\text{leap}=\begin{cases}
  1&{\begin{aligned}
    &\text{ if } (\text{y} + 1)\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod} \ \ \ \ 4=0\\
    &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_conjunction}{\land}(\text{y} + 1)\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod} 100\neq0\\
    &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction}{\lor}(\text{y} + 1)\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod} 400=0\end{aligned}}\\\\
  0&{\text{ otherwise}}\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-leap}

$$\text{syl}=365+\text{leap}$$ {#eq-leap2syl}
:::

:::{.panel-tabset group="language"}
### Julia

```{julia}
function leap(year = 0)
    year += 1
    year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0 || year % 400 == 0
end
leap(2019)
leap(2020)
```

### Observable JavaScript

```{ojs}
function leap(year = 0) {
  year += 1;
  return year % 4 === 0 && year % 100 !== 0 || year % 400 === 0;
}
leap(2019)
leap(2020)
```

### Python

```{python}
def leap(year=2000):
    year += 1
    return year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0 or year % 400 == 0
leap(2019)
leap(2020)
```

### R

```{r}
leap <- function(year = 0) {
  year <- year + 1
  year %% 4 == 0 & year %% 100 != 0 | year %% 400 == 0
}
leap(2019)
leap(2020)
```

:::

Dec categorizes each date as a [countdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countdown#:~:text=a%20sequence%20of%20backward%20counting%20to%20indicate%20the%20time%20remaining%20before%20an%20event%20is%20scheduled%20to%20occur) or countup date, depending on whether the date counts **up** the days **since** Year [y](#y){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year"} or counts **down** the days **until** Year [y](#y){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year"}+1. The current year+day [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} date, [\${decYearColor}[+]{.mono}\${decDotyPadColor}]{.nowrap}, informs us that Year \${decYearColor1} began \${decDotyColor} days ago, whereas its countdown equivalent, [\${nextYearColor}[-]{.mono}\${TminusPaddedColor}]{.nowrap}, tells us that Year \${nextYearColor1} will begin in \${TminusColor} days.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup02}
$$\text{y}+\dfrac{\text{pid}}{\text{syl}} = \text{y} + 1 + \dfrac{\text{nid}}{\text{syl}}$$ {#eq-updown}
:::

Both [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"} and [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer days of year"} can be useful. If we wanted to add 285 days to the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} selected below, for example to predict when a pregnant🤰woman will give birth to a baby👩‍🍼[@jukicLengthHumanPregnancy2013], we should add 285 to the [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} if it is less than 80 in a common year or less than 81 in a leap year, but otherwise we should add 1 to the year and add 285 to the [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"}: \${easyDoyColor} + 285 = \${easySumColor}.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: boundsliders
//| className: sliders
//| code-copy: false
Inputs.bind(Inputs.range([0, 364 + leapInput], {step: 1, label: "Day of year"}), viewof dotyInput)
Inputs.bind(Inputs.range([-365 - leapInput, -1], {step: 1, label: "Day of year"}), viewof dotyInput1)
```

Every [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}, [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of ten days"}, and [dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} has an associated Decolor that can be expressed as a [hexadecimal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_colors#Hex_triplet:~:text=hexadecimal%20number%20used%20in%20HTML%2C%20CSS%2C%20SVG%2C%20and%20other%20computing%20applications%20to%20represent%20colors) ([hex](#hex){#hexadecimal .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hexadecimal"}), "[hue saturation lightness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HSL_and_HSV#:~:text=the%20two%20most%20common%20cylindrical%2Dcoordinate%20representations%20of%20points%20in%20an%20RGB%20color%20model)" ([hsl](#hsl){#huesaturationlightness .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hue saturation lightness"}), or "[[red]{.color0} [green]{.color4} [blue]{.color7}](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RGB_color_model#:~:text=an%20additive%20color%20model)" ([rgb](#rgb){#redgreenblue .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="red green blue"}) triplet. 
Use the "Day of year" range inputs above to choose from the \${nDaysInput} [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}, 37 [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of ten days"}, and 10 [dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} that can be displayed in @tbl-color below and compare their corresponding [hue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hue#:~:text=an%20angular%20position%20around%20a%20central%20or%20neutral%20point%20or%20axis%20on%20a%20color%20space%20coordinate%20diagram) degrees ([h°]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hsl degrees"}) and [hex](#hex){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hexadecimal"} and [rgb](#rgb){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="red green blue"} triplets.

::: {#tbl-color .overflowtable}

| -----------------------------------------------------------------------------| -----------------------| -----------------                                                       | ----------------                                                  | ---------------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------------- |
| [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}      | \${dotyInputColor1}    | \${dotyInputColor2}                                                     | \${dotyInputColor3}                                               | \${dotyInputColor4}    | \${dotyInputColor5}    | \${dotyInputColor6}    |
| [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of ten days"}   | \${dotyInputDekColor1} | \${dotyInputDekColor2}                                                  | \${dotyInputDekColor3}                                            | \${dotyInputDekColor4} | \${dotyInputDekColor5} | \${dotyInputDekColor6} |

:::

The [radio](https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/input-radio) input beneath the plots selects the [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} for [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}\${january1doyColor}, the first day of the Gregorian calendar year. Changing the [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}\${january1doyColor1} [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} shifts every Gregorian calendar date by 1 to 6 days without affecting Decalendar. A leap year that begins on the last [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}, [Dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} [6]{.color6by7}, has an extra "week of year" ([woy](#woy){#weekofyear .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="week of year"}), but its first and last [woy](#woy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="week of year"}, Weeks 0 and 53, each contribute only 1 day to the year.

Even though weeks determine the shape of the Gregorian calendar plot, its cell values are "days of month" ([dom](#dom){#dayofmonth .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of month"}). We can uniquely identify🪪a specific day in any year with a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"}, rather than a month and a [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"}. Except for [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[365]{.color365by366} in leap years, every year has the same [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of ten days"}, [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"}, and months, but not the same weeks. It takes 5, 6, 7, 11, or 12 years for a [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}\${january1doyColor2} [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} to recur.

The number of forms that the Gregorian calendar can take, 14, is the product of 7 [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"} and 2 year lengths. If we set aside an extra copy of a printed🖨️Gregorian calendar on [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}\${january1doyColor3}, we would have to wait 6, 11, 12, 17, 23, 28, or 40 years to use it. We can make the leap year form of Decalendar apply to any year by appending an asterisk (\*) to the label for [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[365]{.color365by366}: [365]{.color0}\*.

The [365]{.color0}\* label is short for [365]{.color0}\*leap, where leap is the [left-hand side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sides_of_an_equation#:~:text=the%20expression%20on%20the%20left%20of%20the%20%22%3D%22%20is%20the%20left%20side%20of%20the%20equation) of @eq-leap. If leap is 1, Year [y](#y){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year"} is a leap year and [365]{.color0}\* is [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[365]{.color365by366}, the last day of Year [y](#y){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year"}. If leap is 0, Year [y](#y){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year"} is a common year and [365]{.color0}\* is [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[0]{.color0}, the first day of Year [y](#y){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year"}+1. The [365]{.color0}\* label unites the common and leap year forms of Decalendar into a [perennial calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perennial_calendar#:~:text=a%20calendar%20that%20applies%20to%20any%20year%2C%20keeping%20the%20same%20dates) that can be reused♻️every year.

# Day of xún (dox) {#sec-dox}

As opposed to a week, an [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of ten days"} can be split evenly into either 5 pairs of days or 2 equal halves called "pentadays of xún" ([pox](#pox){#pentadayofxun .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentadays of xún"}). Likewise, a common year can be divided evenly into 73 groups of 5 days called "pentadays" ([p](#p){#pentaday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentadays"}): [p](#p){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentadays"}[0]{.color0} to [p](#p){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentadays"}[72]{.color360by365}. The last [p](#p){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday"} of a leap year, [p](#p){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday"}[73]{.color365by366}, consists of the final day of the leap year, [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[365]{.color365by366}, and the first 4 days of the subsequent year: [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[0]{.color0} to [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[3]{.color003}.

In the context of a common year, [p](#p){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday"}[73]{.color0} is synonymous with [p](#p){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday"}[0]{.color0} of the succeeding year. To obtain the current [p](#p){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday"}, we divide the current [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"} by 5 and then use the [floor function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floor_and_ceiling_functions#:~:text=the%20function%20that%20takes%20a%20real%20number%20x%20as%20input%20and%20returns%20the%20greatest%20integer%20less%20than%20or%20equal%20to%20x) as in @eq-poy to discard the [fractional part](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractional_part#:~:text=the%20excess%20beyond%20that%20number%27s%20integer%20part) of the quotient: \${decPentColor} = [&LeftFloor;](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractional_part#:~:text=the%20excess%20beyond%20that%20number%27s%20integer%20part){.nounder}\${decDotyColor1} &div; 5[&RightFloor;](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractional_part#:~:text=the%20excess%20beyond%20that%20number%27s%20integer%20part){.nounder}. If we divide a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"} or a [dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} by 5, the remainder will be its corresponding "day of pentaday" ([dop](#dop){#dayofpentaday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of pentaday"}): \${decDotpColor} = \${decDotyColor2} [mod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder) 5. 

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup03}
$$\text{x} = \left\lfloor\dfrac{\text{pid}}{10}\right\rfloor$$ {#eq-xun}
$$\text{dox} = \text{pid} \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod} 10$$ {#eq-dox}
$$\text{pox} = \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{[}\text{dox} > 4\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{]}$$ {#eq-pox}
$$\text{p} = \left\lfloor\dfrac{\text{pid}}{5}\right\rfloor$$ {#eq-poy}
$$\text{dop = dox} \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod} 5$$ {#eq-dop}
:::

In @fig-zero below, each row is a [pox](#pox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday of xún"} and each square node is a [dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"}. @fig-zero visualizes Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"}, a Dec schedule that plans for exactly 219 work days per year, which is about an [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of ten days"} more than the 208 to 210 work days per year provisioned by a [four-day workweek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-day_workweek#:~:text=an%20arrangement%20where%20a%20workplace%20or%20place%20of%20education%20has%20its%20employees%20or%20students%20work%20or%20attend%20school%2C%20college%20or%20university%20over%20the%20course%20of%20four%20days%20per%20week). Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"} designates [Dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} [1]{.color1}, [2]{.color2}, [3]{.color3}, [6]{.color6}, [7]{.color7}, and [8]{.color8} as work days and [Dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} [0]{.color0}, [4]{.color4}, [5]{.color5}, and [9]{.color9} as rest days. 

::: {.centered}

:::

Dec identifies groups of days between [Dop](#dop){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of pentaday"} [0]{.color0} and [4]{.color8} as "pentaday interquintile ranges" ([pir](#pir){#pentadayinterquintilerange .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday interquintile ranges"}): [Dop](#dop){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of pentaday"} [1]{.color2}, [2]{.color4}, and [3]{.color6}. Similarly, the days betwixt [Dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} [0]{.color0} and [9]{.color9} are "xún interdecile ranges" ([xir](#xir){#xuninterdecilerange .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="xún interdecile ranges"}). The names for [pir](#pir){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday interquintile range"} and [xir](#xir){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="xún interdecile range"} are inspired by the terms [quintile](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/quintile#:~:text=quantiles%20which%20divide%20an%20ordered%20sample%20population%20into%20five%20equally%20numerous%20subsets), [decile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decile#:~:text=nine%20values%20that%20divide%20the%20sorted%20data%20into%20ten%20equal%20parts), and [interquartile range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interquartile_range#:~:text=a%20measure%20of%20statistical%20dispersion). If we follow Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"}, a [pir](#pir){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday interquintile ranges"} is to a [workweek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Workweek_and_weekend#:~:text=the%20part%20of%20the%20seven%2Dday%20week%20devoted%20to%20working) as a [p](#p){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday"} is to a week and as an [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of ten days"} is to a [fortnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortnight#:~:text=a%20unit%20of%20time%20equal%20to%2014%20days).

The pair of days between two [pir](#pir){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday interquintile ranges"} is called a "[liminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liminality#:~:text=the%20quality%20of%20ambiguity%20or%20disorientation%20that%20occurs%20in%20the%20middle%20stage%20of%20a%20rite%20of%20passage) interconnecting margin" ([lim](#lim){#liminalinterconnectingmargin .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="liminal interconnecting margin"}). The last [lim](#lim){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="liminal interconnecting margin"} of a common year, [Lim](#lim){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="liminal interconnecting margin"} [73]{.color364by365}, comprises [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[364]{.color364by365} and [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[0]{.color0} and is synonymous with [Lim](#lim){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="liminal interconnecting margin"} [0]{.color364by365} of the subsequent year. In a leap year, [Lim](#lim){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="liminal interconnecting margin"} [73]{.color364by366} consists of [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[364]{.color364by366} and [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[365]{.color365by366} and overlaps with [Lim](#lim){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="liminal interconnecting margin"} [74]{.color365by366}, which is composed of [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[365]{.color365by366} and [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[0]{.color0} and is equivalent to [Lim](#lim){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="liminal interconnecting margin"} [0]{.color365by366} of the ensuing year.

Except for [Lim](#lim){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="liminal interconnecting margin"} [74]{.color365by366}, every even-numbered [lim](#lim){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="liminal interconnecting margin"} is the border that separates two [xir](#xir){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="xún interdecile ranges"}. With the exception of [Lim](#lim){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="liminal interconnecting margin"} [73]{.color364by365}, every odd-numbered [lim](#lim){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="liminal interconnecting margin"} is flanked by the two [pir](#pir){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday interquintile ranges"} within each [xir](#xir){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="xún interdecile range"}. @fig-zerocomm below shows the final five [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"} of a common year and the first five [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"} of the following year, which include the last day of [Lim](#lim){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="liminal interconnecting margin"} [72]{.color359by365}, [Pir](#pir){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday interquintile range"} [72]{.color361by365}, [Lim](#lim){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="liminal interconnecting margin"} [0]{.color364by365}, [Pir](#Pir){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday interquintile range"} [0]{.color001}, and the first day of [Lim](#lim){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="liminal interconnecting margin"} [1]{.color004}.

The diagrams above illustrate that the transition from a common year preserves the alternating pattern of two-day [lim](#lim){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="liminal interconnecting margin"} and three-day [pir](#pir){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday interquintile ranges"}. According to Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"}, [pir](#pir){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday interquintile ranges"} only contain workdays and [lim](#lim){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="liminal interconnecting margin"} are solely made up of rest days. When we follow Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"}, a [lim](#lim){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="liminals"} is the Dec analog of a weekend. To make [lim](#lim){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="liminal interconnecting margin"} appear like weekends we can start from [Dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} [1]{.color1} instead of [Dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} [0]{.color0} as in the @fig-one below, which displays its [lim](#lim){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="liminal interconnecting margin"} as a two-by-two square on the right like [Lim](#lim){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="liminal interconnecting margin"} [73]{.color364by366} and [1]{.color004} in @fig-zeroleap above.

::: {.centered}
### Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"} ([Dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} [1]{.color1} to [0]{.color0}) {.diagtitle}
:::

The order of [dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} in @fig-one is different than all of the previous diagrams but all of the diagrams above show Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"} because the categorization of [dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} as work or rest days remains unchanged. If we left [rotate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circular_shift#:~:text=moving%20the%20final%20entry%20to%20the%20first%20position%2C%20while%20shifting%20all%20other%20entries%20to%20the%20next%20position%2C%20or%20by%20performing%20the%20inverse%20operation) (↺) the [dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} categories of Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"} by 1 day, we get the Schedule [X]{.color28by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal X is decimal 28 or binary 11100"} Dec schedule: [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"} ↺ 1 = [X]{.color28by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal X is decimal 28 or binary 11100"}. Schedule [X]{.color28by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal X is decimal 28 or binary 11100"} groups rest days at the end of each [p](#p){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday"}.

::: {.centered}
### Schedule [X]{.color28by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal X is decimal 28 or binary 11100"} ([Dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} [0]{.color0} to [9]{.color9}) {.diagtitle}

If we adhere to Schedule [X]{.color28by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal X is decimal 28 or binary 11100"}, there will be 4 consecutive work days during any transition from a leap year. To limit the number of consecutive work days to 3, we could right rotate (↻) Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"} and obtain Schedule [F]{.color07by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal F is decimal 7 or binary 00111"}: [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"} ↻ 1 = [F]{.color07by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal F is decimal 7 or binary 00111"}. Unlike Schedule [X]{.color28by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal X is decimal 28 or binary 11100"}, Schedule [F]{.color07by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal F is decimal 7 or binary 00111"} handles yearly transitions just as gracefully as Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"} and provisions the same number of work days per year.

::: {.centered}

:::

There are 32 Dec schedules which can be expressed as a five-bit ([5b]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="five-bit"}) [binary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_number#:~:text=only%20two%20symbols%20for%20the%20natural%20numbers%3A%20typically%200%20%28zero%29%20and%201%20%28one%29) ([[base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radix#:~:text=the%20number%20of%20unique%20digits)2]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="binary"}) sequence. Of these 32 binary sequences, 8 are palindromes. If a Dec schedule can be represented by a [5b]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="five-bit"} palindrome, we can identify its work and rest days by the last digit of not only the [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"} but also either the subsequent [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"} ([ni[d]{.acute}](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="next negative integer day of year"}) in common years or the [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"} after next ([ni[d]{.doubleacute}](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"}) in leap years.

We can sum a [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"} with 1 to get a [ni[d]{.acute}](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="next negative integer day of year"}, [ni[d]{.acute}](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="next negative integer day of year"} = [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"} + 1, or with 2 to get a [ni[d]{.doubleacute}](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="next negative integer day of year"}: [ni[d]{.doubleacute}](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="next negative integer day of year"} = [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"} + 2. @tbl-vincommon below displays the [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"}, [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"}, [ni[d]{.acute}](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="next negative integer day of year"}, and "mixed integer [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}" ([mid](#mid){#mixedintegerdoy .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mixed integer day of year"}) of the first and last 11 days of a common year. We can use the last digit of any [mid](#mid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mixed integer day of year"} that is derived from an [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer days of year"} to discern between the work and rest days of any of the 32 Dec [5b]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="five-bit"} schedules in common years.

The horizontal line above all but the last digit of the [mid](#mid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mixed integer days of year"} in @tbl-vincommon is called a [vinculum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinculum_(symbol)#:~:text=a%20horizontal%20line%20used%20in%20mathematical%20notation%20for%20various%20purposes). In Dec, a vinculum negates whatever is beneath it, negating all of the digits of an integer flips its [sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sign_(mathematics)#:~:text=property%20of%20being%20either%20positive%2C%20negative%2C%20or%200), and a negative integer is denoted by either a vinculum or a [minus sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plus_and_minus_signs#Minus_sign:~:text=When%20it%20is%20placed%20immediately%20before%20an%20unsigned%20number%2C%20the%20combination%20names%20a%20negative%20number%2C%20the%20additive%20inverse%20of%20the%20positive%20number%20that%20the%20numeral%20would%20otherwise%20name). For example, [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[[1]{.overline}]{.color364by365} and [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[[1]{.overline}9]{.color364by365} are two equivalent ways to write Day [-1]{.color364by365}, the last day of the Dec year.

In a common year, the last digits of [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"} and [ni[d]{.acute}](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"} run antiparallel to each other like complementary strands of [deoxyribonucleic acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA#:~:text=a%20polymer%20composed%20of%20two%20polynucleotide%20chains%20that%20coil%20around%20each%20other%20to%20form%20a%20double%20helix)🧬, but in place of [adenine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adenine#:~:text=a%20purine%20nucleotide%20base%20that%20is%20found%20in%20DNA) to [thymine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thymine#:~:text=one%20of%20the%20four%20nucleotide%20bases%20in%20the%20nucleic%20acid%20of%20DNA) and [cytosine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cytosine#:~:text=one%20of%20the%20four%20nucleotide%20bases%20found%20in%20DNA) to [guanine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guanine#:~:text=one%20of%20the%20four%20main%20nucleotide%20bases), the pattern is [0]{.color0} to [[4]{.acute}]{.color5}, [1]{.color1} to [[3]{.acute}]{.color4}, [2]{.color2} to [[2]{.acute}]{.color3}, [3]{.color3} to [[1]{.acute}]{.color2}, [4]{.color4} to [[0]{.acute}]{.color1}, and so on. The final digits of [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"} and [ni[d]{.doubleacute}](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer days of year"} follow the same pattern in leap years: [0]{.color0} to [[4]{.doubleacute}]{.color6}, [1]{.color1} to [[3]{.doubleacute}]{.color5}, [2]{.color2} to [[2]{.doubleacute}]{.color4}, [3]{.color3} to [[1]{.doubleacute}]{.color3}, [4]{.color4} to [[0]{.doubleacute}]{.color2}, and so on.

The last digits of [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"} and [[mi]{.overline}d](#mid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mixed integer days of year"} are misaligned by 4 days in leap years and by 5 days in common years. Dec maintains a constant five-day misalignment by replacing the [[mi]{.overline}d](#mid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mixed integer days of year"} with the next [[mi]{.overline}d](#mid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mixed integer days of year"} ([[mi]{.overline}[d]{.grave}](#mid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="next mixed integer day of year"}) in leap years. The accents above [ni[d]{.acute}](#mid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"} and [[mi]{.overline}[d]{.grave}](#mid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="next mixed integer day of year"} both advance the apparent [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} by one day. @tbl-vinculeap below shows the [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"}, [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"}, [ni[d]{.doubleacute}](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"}, and [[mi]{.overline}[d]{.grave}](#mid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="next mixed integer day of year"} of the first and last 11 days of a leap year.

:::::

A digit can be negated by a vinculum, augmented by an [acute accent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acute_accent#:~:text=a%20diacritic%20used%20in%20many%20modern%20written%20languages%20with%20alphabets%20based%20on%20the%20Latin%2C%20Cyrillic%2C%20and%20Greek%20scripts), diminished by a [grave accent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grave_accent#:~:text=a%20diacritical%20mark%20used%20to%20varying%20degrees%20in%20French%2C%20Dutch%2C%20Portuguese%2C%20Italian%2C%20Catalan%20and%20many%20other%20Western%20European%20languages), double augmented by a double acute accent, or double diminished by a double grave accent. The main purpose of these modifications is to change the appearance of the last digit of an [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"} so that it matches the work or rest day classification of the last digit of a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"}.

The Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"} rule for categorization of work and rest days can be summarized as [\[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise){.nounder}[dop](#dop){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of pentaday"} ∈ {[1]{.color2},[2]{.color4},[3]{.color6}}[\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise){.nounder}, where ∈ means "is an element of" and {[1]{.color2},[2]{.color4},[3]{.color6}} is Set [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"}, a [set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics)#:~:text=a%20set%20is-,a%20collection%20of%20different%20things,-%5B1%5D) which contains all of the [dop]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of pentaday"} that are Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"} work days. The Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"} rule can be applied to the last digit of the [[mi]{.overline}d]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="next mixed integer day of year"} or [ni[d]{.acute}]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mixed integer day of year"} in common years, of the [[mi]{.overline}[d]{.grave}]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="next mixed integer day of year"} or [ni[d]{.doubleacute}]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mixed integer day of year"} in leap years, or of the [pid]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"} in all years.

## Base32 {#b32 .hiddenheading}

Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"} can be expressed in Dec [duotrigesimal](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/duotrigesimal#:~:text=Based%20upon%20the%20number%20thirty%2Dtwo) ([base32]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal"}) as [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"}, in [decimal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal#:~:text=a%20numeral%20system%20that%20uses%20ten%20as%20its%20radix%20%28base%29) ([base10]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="decimal"}) as [14]{.color14by32}, or in [base2]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="binary"} as [01110]{.color14by32}, where 0 is a rest day and 1 is a work day. Any of the 32 Dec [5b]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="five-bit"} schedules can be represented by a single letter of the Dec base32 ([b32]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec base32"}) alphabet. The [b32]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec base32"} letters are listed in @tbl-b32 below alongside their base10 ([b10]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec base10"}) and base2 ([b2]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec base2"}) equivalents.

@tbl-b32 above shows that the [b32]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="the Dec base32"} alphabet includes the 26 letters of the [English alphabet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_alphabet#:~:text=a%20Latin%2Dscript%20alphabet%20consisting%20of%2026%C2%A0letters) and combines the 6 [vowels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vowel#:~:text=a%20speech%20sound%20pronounced%20without%20any%20stricture%20in%20the%20vocal%20tract), [A]{.color0}, [E]{.color05by32}, [I]{.color10by32}, [O]{.color17by32}, [U]{.color24by32}, and [Y]{.color29by32}, with acute accents ( ́) to create 6 additional letters, [[A]{.acute}]{.color01by32}, [[E]{.acute}]{.color05by32}, [[I]{.acute}]{.color11by32}, [[O]{.acute}]{.color18by32}, [[U]{.acute}]{.color25by32}, and [[Y]{.acute}]{.color30by32}, for a total of 32 letters. The 6 additional accented letters are included immediately after their unaccented antecedents as per the order of the English alphabet.
