If we need more work days than those provided by Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"}, we can switch to the Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"}[M]{.color15by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal M is decimal 15 or binary 01111"} Dec ten-bit ([10b]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="ten-bit"}) schedule by following Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"} on even numbered [p](#p){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentadays"} and Schedule [M]{.color15by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal M is decimal 17 or binary 01111"} on odd numbered [p](#p){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentadays"}. Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"}[M]{.color15by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal M is decimal 15 or binary 01111"} has 1 more work day per [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of ten days"} than Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"} and provisions 255 work days per year without modifying the yearly transition shown in Diagrams -@fig-zerocomm and -@fig-zeroleap above.

In contrast to weekly schedules, Dec schedules like [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="L in base32 is 14 in base10 and 01110 in base2"} and [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="L in base32 is 14 in base10 and 01110 in base2"}[M]{.color15by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="M in base32 is 15 in base10 and 01111 in base2"} produce a consistent🎯number of work days every year. While Days [364]{.color364by365}, [365]{.color365by366}, and [0]{.color0} can be work or rest days in the Gregorian calendar️, these days are always rest days if we comply with Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="L in base32 is 14 in base10 and 01110 in base2"} or [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="L in base32 is 14 in base10 and 01110 in base2"}[M]{.color15by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="M in base32 is 15 in base10 and 01111 in base2"}. Therefore, Schedules [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="L in base32 is 14 in base10 and 01110 in base2"} and [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="L in base32 is 14 in base10 and 01110 in base2"}[M]{.color15by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="M in base32 is 15 in base10 and 01111 in base2"} do not require any holidays to smooth the transition between years.

There are 11 United States (US) [Federal holidays](https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/pay-leave/federal-holidays/). US Federal holidays that fall on a Gregorian calendar️ rest day, [Dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} [0]{.color0 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Sunday"} or [Dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} [6]{.color6by7 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Saturday"}, are observed on the nearest Gregorian calendar️ work day: [Dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} [1]{.color1by7 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Monday"} or [Dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} [5]{.color5by7 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Friday"}. Rather than apply this rule to Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"} and move holidays from [Dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} [0]{.color0} to [1]{.color1}, [4]{.color4} to [3]{.color3}, [5]{.color5} to [6]{.color6}, or [9]{.color9} to [8]{.color8}, we can switch between Dec schedules as needed.

Over the course of a Dec cycle, which consists of 400 years, 20871 weeks, or 146097 days, a five-day workweek provides an average of 260.8875 work days per year. If we round 260.8875 to 261 and then subtract the 11 US Federal holidays, we get an annual total of 250 work days, which is 1 [p](#p){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday"} less than the total work days provided annually by Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"}[M]{.color15by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal M is decimal 15 or binary 01111"}.

The yearly work day total of Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"}[M]{.color15by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal M is decimal 15 or binary 01111"} would be 249 if Days [19]{.color019}, [111]{.color111by365}, [149]{.color149by365}, [206]{.color206by365}, [296]{.color296by365}, and [316]{.color316by365} were reclassified as rest days. Approximately, [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[19]{.color019} is the [northward equinox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/March_equinox#:~:text=the%20equinox%20on%20the%20Earth%20when%20the%20subsolar%20point%20appears%20to%20leave%20the%20Southern%20Hemisphere%20and%20cross%20the%20celestial%20equator%2C%20heading%20northward%20as%20seen%20from%20Earth), [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[111]{.color111by365} is the [northern solstice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/June_solstice#:~:text=the%20solstice%20on%20Earth%20that%20occurs%20annually%20between%2020%20and%2022%20June%20according%20to%20the%20Gregorian%20calendar), [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[149]{.color149by365} is the hottest [doy](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"} globally on average, [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[206]{.color206by365} is the [southward equinox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_equinox#:~:text=the%20moment%20when%20the%20Sun%20appears%20to%20cross%20the%20celestial%20equator%2C%20heading%20southward), [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[296]{.color296by365} is the [southern solstice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/December_solstice#:~:text=the%20solstice%20that%20occurs%20each%20December%20%E2%80%93%20typically%20on%2021%20December), and [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[316]{.color316by365} is the coldest [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"} globally on average.

The last US Federal holiday of the Gregorian calendar year is [Christmas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas#:~:text=annual%20festival%20commemorating%20the%20birth%20of%20Jesus%20Christ)🎄. Although it occurs on [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[299]{.color299by365}, which is the last day of [Hectoday]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hundreds of days"} [2]{.color200by365} ([h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"}[2]{.color200by365}), Christmas is likely to be celebrated on [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[300]{.color300by365}, the first day of [Hectoday]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hundreds of days"} [3]{.color300by365} ([h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"}[3]{.color300by365}), by people who do not use Dec and live in a UTC time zone with a negative offset. The Dec analog of the [holiday season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas_and_holiday_season#:~:text=an%20annual%20period%20generally%20spanning%20from%20November%20or%20December%20to%20early%20January%20incorporating%20Christmas%20Day%20and%20New%20Year%27s%20Day) is [Hectoday]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hundreds of days"} [-1]{.color265by365} ([h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"}[[1]{.overline}]{.color265by365}). 

# Day of hectoday (doh) {#sec-doh}

[Astronomical seasons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Season#Astronomical) vary in duration. The length of a meterological season is 2 months in the [Hindu calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu_calendar#Solar_months_and_seasons:~:text=approximate%20correspondence%20to-,Hindu%20seasons,-%28%E1%B9%9Atu%29%20and), 3 months in the Gregorian calendar, 3 months, 9 [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of ten days"}, or 90 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} in the [French Revolutionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Republican_calendar#Design:~:text=There%20were%20twelve%20months%2C%20each%20divided%20into%20three%2010%2Dday%20weeks%20called%20d%C3%A9cades) calendar, 4 months, 12 [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of ten days"}, or 120 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} in the [Egyptian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian_calendar#:~:text=Each%20season%20was%20divided%20into%20four%20months%20of%2030%20days.%20These%20twelve%20months%20were%20initially%20numbered%20within%20each%20season%20but%20came%20to%20also%20be%20known%20by%20the%20names%20of%20their%20principal%20festivals.%20Each%20month%20was%20divided%20into%20three%2010%2Dday%20periods%20known%20as%20decans%20or%20decades) calendar, 13 weeks or 91 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} in the [World Season Calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Asimov#Calendar:~:text=divides%20the%20year%20into%20four%20seasons%20%28named%20A%E2%80%93D%29%20of%2013%20weeks%20%2891%20days%29%20each), and 1 [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"}, 10 [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of ten days"}, 20 [p](#p){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentadays"}, or 100 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} in Decalendar.

As opposed to seasons in other calendars, the 4 Dec seasons are chosen from 2 overlapping sets of 4 consecutive [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"}, called "positive integer hectodays" ([pih](#pih){#positiveintegerhectoday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer hectodays"}) and "negative integer hectodays" ([nih](#nih){#negativeintegerhectoday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer hectodays"}), to match [daily global mean temperature](https://pulse.climate.copernicus.eu) patterns. Every [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"} is simultaneously a member of a [pih](#pih){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer hectoday"}, [nih]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer hectoday"}, "positive integer xún" ([pix](#pix){#positiveintegerxun .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer xún"}), and "negative integer xún" ([nix](#nix){#negativeintegerxun .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer xún"}).

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup04}
$$\text{pih} = \left\lfloor\dfrac{\text{pid}}{100}\right\rfloor$$ {#eq-pih}
$$\text{nih} = \left\lfloor\dfrac{\text{nid}}{100}\right\rfloor$$ {#eq-nih}
$$\text{pix} = \left\lfloor\dfrac{\text{pid}}{10}\right\rfloor$$ {#eq-pix}
$$\text{nix} = \left\lfloor\dfrac{\text{nid}}{10}\right\rfloor$$ {#eq-nix}
:::

Day [0]{.color0} is in [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}[0]{.color0}, [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of ten days"}[0]{.color0}, [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}[[4]{.overline}]{.color330by365}, and [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of ten days"}[[37]{.overline}]{.color360by365}. Days [364]{.color364by365} and [365]{.color365by366} are in [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}[3]{.color300by365}, [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of ten days"}[36]{.color360by365}, [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}[[1]{.overline}]{.color265by365}, and [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of ten days"}[[1]{.overline}]{.color355by365}. While [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}[0]{.color0} and [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of ten days"}[0]{.color0} start at the [boy](#boy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of year"}, both [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}[3]{.color300by365} and [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of ten days"}[36]{.color360by365} extend beyond the "end of year" ([eoy](#eoy){#endofyear .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="end of year"}). Conversely, [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}[[4]{.overline}]{.color330by365} and [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of ten days"}[[37]{.overline}]{.color360by365} begin before the [boy](#boy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of year"} but [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}[[1]{.overline}]{.color265by365} and [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of ten days"}[[1]{.overline}]{.color355by365} do not go past the [eoy](#eoy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="end of year"}. The [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of ten days"}[[37]{.overline}]{.color360by365} of any common year is equivalent to and thus has the same color label as the [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of ten days"}[36]{.color360by365} of the prior year.

In Dec, each group of days has the same color label as its first [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"}. Day [365]{.color365by366} does not affect pih and pix color labels but shifts [nih](#nih){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer hectodays"} and [nix](#nix){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer xún"} color labels by 1 day. If the [syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"} is unknown, Dec labels [nih](#nih){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer hectoday"} and [nix](#nix){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer xún"} with common year colors by default. Depending on the year, [woy](#woy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="week of year"} color labels can differ by 1 to 6 days and thus can only be used when the year is known.


The [line](https://observablehq.com/plot/marks/line) chart below labels the 4 Dec seasons, [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"}[0]{.color0}, [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"}[1]{.color100}, [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"}[2]{.color200by365}, and [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"}[[1]{.overline}]{.color265by365}, with their respective colors: [red]{.color0}, [chartreuse]{.color100}, [blue]{.color200by365}, and [violet]{.color265by365}. The [blue]{.color200by365} area denoting [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"}[2]{.color200by365} is truncated to hide its overlap with the [violet]{.color265by365} area signifying [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"}[[1]{.overline}]{.color265by365}. Coincidentally, the [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"}[2]{.color200by365} and [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"}[[1]{.overline}]{.color265by365} overlap begins 1 or 2 days before the soonest possible date of [Thanksgiving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thanksgiving#:~:text=Thanksgiving%20is-,a%20national%20holiday,-celebrated%20on%20various)🦃and ends with [Christmas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas#:~:text=annual%20festival%20commemorating%20the%20birth%20of%20Jesus%20Christ)🎄.

{{< include /dec/date/_season.qmd >}}

The line chart shows [ERA5](https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/datasets/reanalysis-era5-single-levels?tab=overview#:~:text=the%20fifth%20generation%20ECMWF%20reanalysis%20for%20the%20global%20climate%20and%20weather%20for%20the%20past%208%20decades) daily global mean temperatures for every doy.
If we think of the method for assigning [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"} to Dec seasons in @eq-season as a [classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classification#:~:text=the%20activity%20of%20assigning%20objects%20to%20some%20pre%2Dexisting%20classes%20or%20categories) [model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_model#:~:text=a%20mathematical%20model%20that%20embodies%20a%20set%20of%20statistical%20assumptions%20concerning%20the%20generation%20of%20sample%20data), its "[goodness of fit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodness_of_fit#:~:text=a%20statistical%20model%20describes%20how%20well%20it%20fits%20a%20set%20of%20observations)" is supported by the fact that the hottest [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"} on average, [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[149]{.color149by365}, is near the middle of [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"}[1]{.color100} and the coldest [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"} on average, [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[316]{.color316by365}, is close to the center of [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"}[[1]{.overline}]{.color265by365}: [316]{.color316by365} -- 365 = [-49]{.color316by365}.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup05}
$$\text{season} = \left\lfloor\dfrac{\text{pid} - \text{syl} * \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{[}\text{nid} \ge -100\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{]}}{100}\right\rfloor$$ {#eq-season}
:::

In general, the hottest days are in [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}[1]{.color100}, the coldest days are in [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}[[1]{.overline}]{.color265by365}, temperatures increase with time in [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}[0]{.color0}, and temperatures decrease with time in [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}[2]{.color200by365}. Therefore, we can refer to [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}[0]{.color0}, [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}[1]{.color100}, [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}[2]{.color200by365}, and [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"}[[1]{.overline}]{.color265by365} as the rise📈, [crest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crest_and_trough#:~:text=is%20the%20highest%20point%20of%20the%20wave)🔥, fall📉, and [trough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crest_and_trough#:~:text=lowest%20point%20of%20the%20wave)❄️, respectively, of global mean temperatures. @tbl-hoy below shows the Dec season names in the [Northern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Hemisphere#:~:text=half%20of%20Earth%20that%20is%20north%20of%20the%20equator) and [Southern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Hemisphere#:~:text=Earth%20that%20is-,south%20of%20the%20equator,-.%20It%20contains%20all) [Hemispheres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hemispheres_of_Earth#:~:text=any%20division%20of%20the%20globe%20into%20two%20equal%20halves). 

::: {#tbl-hoy .overflowtable}
| Hemisphere |    [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}[0]{.color0}    |    [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}[1]{.color100}    |    [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}[2]{.color200by365}    |    [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}[[1]{.overline}]{.color265by365}    |
| ---------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- |
|  Northern  |  Spring  |  Summer  |  Autumn  |  Winter  |
|  Southern  |  Autumn  |  Winter  |  Spring  |  Summer  |
:::

When we keep the remainder after dividing a [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} by 100, we obtain a "day of hectoday" ([doh](#doh){#dayofhectoday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of hectoday"}), which is the percent of an [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"} that has elapsed. If the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} is a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"}, the [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"} is a [pih](#pih){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer hectoday"}: \${decDotyColor3} mod 100 = \${decDohPidColor}, but if it is an [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"}, the [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"} is a [nih](#nih){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer hectoday"}: [\${TminusColor1}]{.overline} mod 100 = \${decDohNidMidColor}. The [radix complement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Method_of_complements#:~:text=The%20radix%20complement%20of,is%20defined%20as) of the [doh](#doh){#dayofhectoday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of hectoday"} (100--[doh](#doh){#dayofhectoday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of hectoday"}) is the percent of the [pih](#pih){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer hectoday"}, 100 -- \${decDohPidColor1} = \${decDohPidMidColor}, or the [nih](#nih){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer hectoday"}, 100 -- \${decDohNidMidColor1} = \${decDohNidColor}, that is left.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup06}
$$\text{doh} = \text{doy} \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod} 100$$ {#eq-doh}
:::

Similarly, a [dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} is the number of days in an [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of ten days"} that have passed and the radix complement of a [dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} (10--[dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"}) is the number of days in the [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of ten days"} that remain. The [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} in a year+day Dec date is [zero padded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padding_(cryptography)#Zero_padding:~:text=be%20padded%20are-,padded%20with%20zero,-.%20The%20zero%20padding) to three digits. If the three-digit [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} is a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"}:  \${decDotyPadColor1}, its first digit is a [pih](#pih){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer hectoday"}: \${decPih}, its last two digits are a [doh](#doh){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of hectoday"}: \${decDohPidColor2}, its first two digits are a [pix](#pix){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer xún"}: \${decDekColor}, and its final digit is a [dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"}: \${decDotdColor}.

Whereas a pid gives us information on the current [pix](#pix){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer xún"} and [pih](#pih){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer hectoday"}, an [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"} tells us about the [nix](#nix){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer xún"} and [nih](#nih){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer hectoday"} that either are coming up next or began today. The three-digit [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"} in a year+day Dec date, [\${TminusColor3}]{.overline}, presents an [nih](#nih){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer hectoday"} with its first digit: [\${decNihPlus1Color}]{.overline}, 
the days until that [nih](#nih){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer hectoday"} with its last two digits: [\${decDohNidColor1}]{.overline}, an [nix](#nix){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer xún"} with its first two digits: [\${decNixPlus1Color}]{.overline}, and the days until that [nix](#nix){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer xún"} with its final digit: [\${decDoxNidColor}]{.overline}.

An [nih](#nih){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer hectoday"} [mid](#mid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mixed integer day of year"}, [\${decNihAbsColor}]{.overline}\${decDohNidMidPadColor}, shows the current [nih](#nih){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer hectoday"} with its first digit: [\${decNihAbsColor1}]{.overline}, a [doh](#doh){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of hectoday"} with its final two digits: \${decDohNidMidPadColor1}, an [nih](#nih){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer hectoday"} "mixed integer xún" ([mix](#mix){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mixed integer xún"}) with its first two digits: [\${decNihAbsColor2}]{.overline}\${decDohNidMidFirstColor}, and a [dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} with its last digit: \${decDoxNidMidColor}. During [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}[[1]{.overline}]{.color265by365}, Dec recommends using [nih](#nih){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer hectoday"} [mid](#mid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mixed integer day of year"} in lieu of [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} for personal timekeeping because [nih](#nih){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer hectodays"} [mid](#mid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mixed integer day of year"} take into account the [syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"} and thus avoid any uncertainty regarding the [eoy](#eoy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="end of year"}.

Conversion of a [nih](#nih){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer hectoday"} [mix](#mix){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mixed integer xún"} to a [nix](#nix){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer xún"} only requires simple arithmetic: [\${decNihAbsColor3}]{.overline}\${decDohNidMidFirstColor1} = -\${decNihAbsColor4}[0]{.color0} + \${decDohNidMidFirstColor2} = [\${decNixAbsColor}]{.overline}. If we then append a [dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"}, we get a [nix](#nix){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer xún"} [mid](#mid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mixed integer day of year"} like those in @tbl-vincommon: [\${decNixAbsColor1}]{.overline}\${decDoxNidMidColor1}. During a leap year, we should put a grave accent above the [dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} in [nih](#nih){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer hectoday"} and [nix](#nix){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer xún"} [mid](#mid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mixed integer days of year"} as in @tbl-vinculeap to facilitate identification of work and rest days based on a Dec schedule such as Schedule [L]{.color14by32 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duotrigesimal L is decimal 14 or binary 01110"}: [\${decNihGraveColor}]{.overline}\${decDohGraveFirstColor}[\${decDoxGraveColor}]{.grave} = [\${decNixGraveColor}]{.overline}[\${decDoxGraveColor1}]{.grave} = [\${decNihAbsColor5}]{.overline}\${decDohNidMidPadColor2} = [\${decNixPlus1Color1}]{.overline}\${decDoxNidMidColor2}.

We can see that [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}\${decPihColor} is \${decDohPidColor3}% done from the current [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"}: \${decDotyColor4}, [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}\${decPihPlus1Color} will begin after the remaining \${decDohPidMidColor1}% of [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}\${decPih} expires from the current [pih](#pih){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer hectoday"} [mid](#mid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mixed integer day of year"}: \${decPihPlus1Color1}[\${decDohPidMidPadColor}]{.overline}, [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}[\${decNihPlus1Color1}]{.overline} will start once the residual \${decDohNidColor2}% of [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}[\${decNihAbsColor6}]{.overline} elapses from the current [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"}: [\${TminusColor2}]{.overline}, and [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"}[\${decNihAbsColor7}]{.overline} is \${decDohNidMidPadColor3}% finished from the current [nih](#nih){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer hectoday"} [mid](#mid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mixed integer day of year"}: [\${decNihAbsColor8}]{.overline}\${decDohNidMidPadColor4}. The last digit of the [doh](#doh){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of hectoday"} is the [dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} and the final digit of the 100--[doh](#doh){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of hectoday"} is the (10 -- [dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"}) [mod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder) 10.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup07}
$$\text{dox} = \text{doh} \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod} 10$$ {#eq-doh2dox}
:::

Any kind of [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"} can each be split into either an [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of ten days"} and [dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} or an [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="group of one hundred days"} and [doh](#doh){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of hectoday"}, but the vinculum in a [mid](#mid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mixed integer day of year"} can can be used to emphasize one of these two options. If we want to categorize work and rest days based on [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"} as in the Gregorian calendar instead of [dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} as in Decalendar, we can translate the "day of [era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calendar_era#:~:text=the%20period%20of%20time%20elapsed%20since%20one%20epoch%20of%20a%20calendar)" ([doe](#doe){#dayofera .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of era"}) equivalent of a year+day Dec date into a [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"}. 

# Day of era (doe) {#sec-doe}

Dec refers to midnight on [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[0]{.color0} as the "beginning of year" ([boy](#boy){#beginningofyear .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of year"}). At the [boy](#boy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of year"}, the [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} [rolls over](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rollover#:~:text=the%20act%20of%20a%20counter%20restarting%20its%20count%20sequence) from [364]{.color364by365} or [365]{.color365by366} to [0]{.color0}. If the [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"} did not reset to [-365]{.color0} or [-366]{.color0} at the [boy](#boy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of year"}, it would continue from [[1]{.overline}]{.color364by365} to [0]{.color0} and thus become a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"}. The [doe](#doe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of era"} is like a [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"} that became a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} at the "beginning of era" ([boe](#boe){#beginningofera .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of era"}), midnight on [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[0]{.color0} of Year [0]{.color0} (y[0]{.color0}), and never restarted before or after the [boe](#boe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of era"}.

Each of the ten Dec time zones has its own [boe](#boe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of era"}, [doe](#doe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of era"}, [boy](#boy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of year"}, and [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}. The [boe](#boe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of era"} of the Zone [0]{.color0} ([z](#z){#zone .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="zone"}[0]{.color0}) Dec time zone is called the Dec [epoch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epoch#:~:text=an%20instant%20in%20time%20chosen%20as%20the%20origin%20of%20a%20particular%20calendar%20era). We can convert [Julian day numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_day#:~:text=a%20continuous%20count%20of%20days%20from%20the%20beginning%20of%20the%20Julian%20period) ([JDN](#jdn){#Juliandaynumber .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Julian day numbers"}) to [z]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="zone"}[0]{.color0} [doe](#doe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of era"} by subtracting the number of full days in between the start of the [Julian period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_day#Terminology:~:text=a%20chronological%20interval%20of%207980%C2%A0years) and the Dec epoch, which is 1721119 if the [z]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="zone"}[0]{.color0} time is later than noon and 1721120 otherwise.

Dec uses [doe](#doe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of era"} for [calendrical calculations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calendrical_calculation#:~:text=a%20calculation%20concerning%20calendar%20dates), such as finding the [POSIX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/POSIX#:~:text=a%20family%20of%20standards%20specified%20by%20the%20IEEE%20Computer%20Society%20for%20maintaining%20compatibility%20between%20operating%20systems) [zero-based [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/007904875/utilities/date.html#:~:text=weekday%20as%20a%20decimal%20number%20%5B0%2C6%5D%20(0%3Dsunday)) of a given date. This year, the [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} of Christmas is \${xmasDotwColor} according to @eq-dow: (\${xmasDote} + \${3 - nOffInput}) [mod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder) 7 = \${xmasDotwColor1}. Unlike [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"}, [dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} can be found without much effort. The [dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} is the last digit of the [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} or equivalently the remainder after dividing the [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} by 10 as per @eq-dox: [299]{.color299by365} [mod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder) 10 = [9]{.color9}.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup08}
$$\text{dow} = (\text{doe} + 3 - \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{[}\text{UTC offset} < 0\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{]}) \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod} 7$$ {#eq-dow}
:::

@eq-dow is adapted from [Howard Hinnant](https://howardhinnant.github.io)'s [`weekday_from_days`](https://howardhinnant.github.io/date_algorithms.html#weekday_from_days) algorithm -@hinnant2021date. The Dec epoch [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} is [3]{.color3by7} = (0 + 3) [mod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder) 7. The [UNIX epoch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix_time#:~:text=00%3A00%3A00%20UTC%20on%201%C2%A0January%201970) [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} is [4]{.color4by7} = (719468 + 3) [mod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder) 7. Depending on how [mod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder) is [defined](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#Variants_of_the_definition), a negative [doe](#doe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of era"} could yield a negative [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}. We can add 7 to a negative [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} in the bottom row of @tbl-dow to obtain the positive [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} above it.

::: {#tbl-dow .overflowtable}
|            | Sun            | Mon               | Tue               | Wed               | Thu               | Fri               | Sat              |
| ---------- | -------------- | ----------------- | ----------------- | ----------------- | ----------------- | ----------------- | ---------------- |
| [+]{.mono} |  [0]{.color0}  |  [1]{.color1by7}  |  [2]{.color2by7}  |  [3]{.color3by7}  |  [4]{.color4by7}  |  [5]{.color5by7}  |  [6]{.color6by7} |
| [-]{.mono} |  [7]{.color0}  |  [6]{.color1by7}  |  [5]{.color2by7}  |  [4]{.color3by7}  |  [3]{.color4by7}  |  [2]{.color5by7}  |  [1]{.color6by7} |
:::

Christmas is an anchored⚓️holiday because it occurs on the same [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} every year. In contrast, floating🛟holidays like Thanksgiving are always planned for the same [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} and thus can fall on various [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"}. We can use @eq-dowdif, which is inspired by [Howard Hinnant](https://howardhinnant.github.io)'s [`weekday_difference`](https://howardhinnant.github.io/date_algorithms.html#weekday_difference) algorithm, to find the floating holiday date in a given year -@hinnant2021date.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup09}
$$\text{dow}_\Delta = (\text{dow}_\text{M} - \text{dow}_\text{S} + 7) \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod} 7$$ {#eq-dowdif}
:::

In @eq-dowdif, [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}~M~ is the [minuend](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/minuend#:~:text=A%20number%20or%20quantity%20from%20which%20another%20is%20to%20be%20subtracted), [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}~S~ is the [subtrahend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtraction#:~:text=number%20being%20subtracted), and [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}~Δ~ is the [difference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtraction#Notation_and_terminology:~:text=The%20result%20is%20the%20difference) between them that ranges from 0 to 6. To get the [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} of the first [Dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} [4]{.color4by7 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Thursday"} after [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[266]{.color266by365}, which is Thanksgiving in the United States🇺🇸and Brazil🇧🇷, we plug [4]{.color4by7} as [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}~M~ and the [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} of [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[267]{.color267by365} as [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}~S~ into @eq-dowdif, \${day266dotwDiffColor} = ([4]{.color4by7} [-]{.mono} \${day266dotwColor} + 7) [mod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder) 7, and then add 267: \${day266dotwDiffPlus267Color} = \${day266dotwDiffColor1} + [267]{.color267by365}.

::: {.callout-warning}
# Bad Pun Alert
[**Deck**aday the halls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deck_the_Halls#:~:text=a%20traditional%20Christmas%20carol.) with [**dow~S~**]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"} of holly! Fa + la &times; 8! 'Tis the **[hectoday]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hundred days"}** to be jolly! Aren't you thankful that I couldn’t *thank* of a Thanksgiving pun?
:::

When the current pid is the minuend and [299]{.color299by365} is the subtrahend, the difference is the number of days *until* [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[299]{.color299by365} if it is negative or the days *since* [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[299]{.color299by365} if it is positive. The current difference tells us that \${xmasDiffColor} days \${xmasDiffSince} [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[299]{.color299by365} of this year: \${decYearColor2}+[299]{.color299by365}[\${xmasDiffSign}]{.mono}\${xmasDiffColor1}. We can then subtract the [syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"} to get the number of days until [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[299]{.color299by365} of next year: \${nextYearColor2}+[299]{.color299by365}[-]{.mono}\${xmasNextColor}.

# Year of era (yoe) {#sec-yoe}

To obtain a [doe](#doe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of era"} that we can plug into @eq-dow, we can use the two components of a Dec year+day date, namely a "year of era" ([yoe](#yoe){#yearofera .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"}) and a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"}, to solve Equations -@eq-yoe2coe, -@eq-yoe2yoc, -@eq-date2doc, and -@eq-doe, which are based on [Howard Hinnant](https://howardhinnant.github.io)'s [`days_from_civil`](https://howardhinnant.github.io/date_algorithms.html#days_from_civil){.mono .under} algorithm that he describes in his manuscript entitled [[`chrono`]{.mono .under}-Compatible Low-Level Date Algorithms](https://howardhinnant.github.io/date_algorithms.html) -@hinnant2021date.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup10}
$$\text{coe} = \biggl \lfloor \frac{\text{yoe}-399\ast\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{[}\text{yoe} \geq 0\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{]}}{400} \biggr \rfloor$$ {#eq-yoe2coe}

$$\text{yoc} = \text{yoe} - \text{coe} \ast 400$$ {#eq-yoe2yoc}

$$\text{doc} = \text{yoc} \ast 365 + \left\lfloor\frac{\text{yoc}}{4}\right\rfloor - \left\lfloor\frac{\text{yoc}}{100}\right\rfloor + \text{pid}$$ {#eq-date2doc}

$$\text{doe} = \text{coe} \ast 146097 + \text{doc}$$ {#eq-doe}
:::

:::{.panel-tabset group="language"}
### Julia

```{julia}
function doe(year = 1969, pid = 306)
    coe = fld(year, 400)
    yoe = year - coe * 400
    return coe * 146097 +
           yoe * 365 +
           fld(yoe, 4) -
           fld(yoe, 100) +
           pid
end
doe()
```

### Observable JavaScript

```{ojs}
function doe(year = 1969, pid = 306) {
  const coe = Math.floor(year / 400),
        yoe = year - coe * 400;
  return coe * 146097 +
    yoe * 365 +
    Math.floor(yoe / 4) -
    Math.floor(yoe / 100) +
    pid
}
doe()
```

### Python

```{python}
def doe(year=1969, pid=306):
    coe = year // 400
    yoe = year - coe * 400
    return (
        coe * 146097
        + yoe * 365
        + yoe // 4
        - yoe // 100
        + pid
    )
doe()
```

### R

```{r}
doe <- function(year = 1969, pid = 306) {
  coe <- year %/% 400
  yoe <- year - coe * 400
  coe * 146097 +
    yoe * 365 +
    yoe %/% 4 -
    yoe %/% 100 +
    pid
}
doe()
```

:::

Equations -@eq-doe2coe, -@eq-doe2doc, -@eq-doe2yoc, -@eq-yoe, and -@eq-doe2pid below are based on [Howard Hinnant](https://howardhinnant.github.io)'s [`civil_from_days`](https://howardhinnant.github.io/date_algorithms.html#civil_from_days){.mono} algorithm and useful for obtaining Dec dates from [doe](#doe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of era"}, [UNIX timestamps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix_time#:~:text=the%20number%20of%20seconds%20that%20have%20elapsed%20since%2000%3A00%3A00%20UTC%20on%201%C2%A0January%201970), and [JDN](#jdn){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Julian day numbers"} -@hinnant2021date. Regardless of whether we convert a [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"} and [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} to a [doe](#doe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of era"} or *vice versa*, along the way we calculate the "[cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_cycle_(calendar)#:~:text=the%20Gregorian%20cycle%20of%20400%20years%20has%20exactly%20146%2C097%20days%2C%20i.e.%20exactly%2020%2C871%20weeks%2C%20one%20can%20say%20that%20the%20Gregorian%20so%2Dcalled%20solar%20cycle%20lasts%20400%20years) of era" ([coe](#coe){#cycleofera .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="cycle of era"}), "year of cycle" ([yoc](#yoc){#yearofcycle .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of cycle"}), and "day of cycle" ([doc](#doc){#dayofcycle .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of cycle"}).

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup11}
$$\text{coe} = \left \lfloor \frac{\text{doe}-146096\ast\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{[}\text{doe} \geq 0\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{]}}{146097} \right \rfloor$$ {#eq-doe2coe}

$$\text{doc} = \text{doe} - \text{coe} \ast 146097$$ {#eq-doe2doc}

$$\text{yoc} = \Biggl \lfloor \frac{\text{doc} - \left\lfloor \dfrac{\text{doc}}{1460} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor \dfrac{\text{doc}}{36524} \right\rfloor - \left\lfloor \dfrac{\text{doc}}{146096} \right\rfloor}{365} \Biggr \rfloor$$ {#eq-doe2yoc}

$$\text{yoe} = \text{yoc} + \text{coe} \ast 400$$ {#eq-yoe}

$$\text{pid} = \text{doc} - \text{yoc} \ast 365 - \left \lfloor \frac{\text{yoc}}{4} \right \rfloor + \left \lfloor \frac{\text{yoc}}{100} \right \rfloor$$ {#eq-doe2pid}
:::

:::{.panel-tabset group="language"}
### Julia

```{julia}
function date(doe = 719468)
    coe = fld(doe, 146097)
    doc = doe - coe * 146097
    yoc = fld(
        doc -
        fld(doc, 1460) +
        fld(doc, 36524) -
        fld(doc, 146096),
        365
    )
    return (
        yoc + coe * 400,
        doc - (
            yoc * 365 +
            fld(yoc, 4) -
            fld(yoc, 100)
        )
    )
end
date()
```

### Observable JavaScript

```{ojs}
function date(doe = 719468) {
  const coe = Math.floor(doe / 146097),
    doc = doe - coe * 146097,
    yoc = Math.floor(
      (
        doc
        - Math.floor(doc / 1460)
        + Math.floor(doc / 36524)
        - Math.floor(doc / 146096)
      ) / 365
    );
  return [
    yoc + coe * 400,
    doc - (
      yoc * 365 +
      Math.floor(yoc / 4) -
      Math.floor(yoc / 100)
    )
  ];
}
date()
```

### Python

```{python}
def date(doe=719468):
    coe = doe // 146097
    doc = doe - coe * 146097
    yoc = (
        doc
        - doc // 1460
        + doc // 36524
        - doc // 146096
    ) // 365
    return (
        yoc + coe * 400,
        doc - (
            yoc * 365 +
            yoc // 4 -
            yoc // 100
        )
    )
date()
```

### R

```{r}
date <- function(doe = 719468) {
  coe <- doe %/% 146097
  doc <- doe - coe * 146097
  yoc <- (
    doc -
    doc %/% 1460 +
    doc %/% 36524 -
    doc %/% 146096
  ) %/% 365
  c(
    yoc + coe * 400,
    doc - (
      yoc * 365 +
      yoc %/% 4 -
      yoc %/% 100
    )
  )
}
date()
```

:::

Dates generated by Equations -@eq-doe2coe, -@eq-doe2doc, -@eq-doe2yoc, -@eq-yoe, and -@eq-doe2pid are guaranteed to be in the standard [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"}+[pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} format. Therefore, we can standardize Dec dates by converting them to [doe](#doe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of era"} and then back to dates again. A [round-trip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round-trip_format_conversion#:~:text=converting%20from%20any%20data%20representation%20and%20back%20again) "date to [doe](#doe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of era"} to date" conversion ensures that the [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"} is an integer and the [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} is a positive integer less than the [syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"}: [0]{.color0} &le; [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} &lt; [syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"}. 

# Day of week (dow) {#sec-dow}

Even though Decalendar functions best with [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of ten days"}, Dec dates can display [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"} by splitting a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} into a "beginning of week" ([bow](#bow){#beginningofweek .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of week"}) and the POSIX zero-based [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}. To obtain the [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of week"}, we subtract the [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} from the [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"}: [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of week"} = [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} [-]{.mono} [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}. According to the current [z]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="zone"}[0]{.color0} [[yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"}+[bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of week"}+[dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}]{.nowrap} date, [\${decYearColor3}[\${dotw0sign}]{.mono}\${dotw0dotyColor1}+\${dotwColor}]{.nowrap}, the most recent [Dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"} [0]{.color0} was on [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}\${dotw0dotyColor2} and today is [Dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"} \${dotwColor1}.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup12}
$$\text{yoe} + \frac{\text{pid}}{\text{syl}} = \text{yoe} + \frac{\text{bow + dow}}{\text{syl}}$$ {#eq-bow}
:::

A Dec [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of week"} date can have a countup or a countdown [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of week"}. The countdown equivalent of [\${decYearColor4}[\${dotw0sign}]{.mono}\${dotw0dotyColor3}+\${dotwColor2}]{.nowrap} is [\${nextYearColor3}[-]{.mono}\${dotw0dotyNegColor}+\${dotwColor3}]{.nowrap}. Like [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"}, countdown [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of week"} can be useful. We can add up to 52 weeks to any countdown [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of week"} without having to take into account the length of the year. The sum of 52 weeks and the last [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of week"}+[dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"} of this year is 52 &times; 7 + ${decYearLastBowNegColor} + \${decYearLastDowColor} = \${decYearLastBowSumColor} + \${decYearLastDowColor1}.

Based on the calculation above, the Dec [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of week"} date that is 52 weeks after [\${nextYearColor4}[-]{.mono}\${decYearLastBowNegColor1}[+]{.mono}\${decYearLastDowColor2}]{.nowrap} is [\${nextYearColor5}[+]{.mono}\${decYearLastBowSumColor1}[+]{.mono}\${decYearLastDowColor3}]{.nowrap}. When we see the same [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"} in two dates, we know that difference between them is a multiple of 7. The [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of week"} can be used to refer to the current week in phrases like "the week of [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}\${dotw0dotyColor4}" or "the week that begins with [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}\${dotw0dotyColor5}" and thus can function like a [woy](#woy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="week of year"}.

We can convert between the [[bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of week"}+[dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}]{.nowrap} in Dec [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of week"} dates and the [7&times;[woy](#woy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="week of year"}+[dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}[-]{.mono}[boy](#boy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of year"}[dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}]{.nowrap} in Dec [woy](#woy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="week of year"} dates. The [boy](#boy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of year"}[dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} is the [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} of the first day of the Dec year. To obtain the current [woy](#woy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="week of year"}, we sum the [boy](#boy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of year"}[dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} with the current [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of week"} and then divide by 7: \${woyColor} = (\${doty0dotwColor} + \${dotw0dotyColor6}) &div; 7. Dec truncates [woy](#woy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="week of year"} dates so that they only display the [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"}, [woy](#woy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="week of year"}, and [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}: \${decYearColor5}[+]{.mono}\${woyColor1}[+]{.mono}\${dotwColor4}.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup13}
$$\text{bow} = 7\ast\text{woy}-\text{boydow}$$ {#eq-woy}
:::

If [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"} were like [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"} and reset at the [boy](#boy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of year"}, the [boy](#boy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of year"}[dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} would always be zero and conversion between [woy](#woy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="week of year"} and [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of week"} dates would be straightforward but the reality is that we need the [boy](#boy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of year"}[dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} to convert a [woy](#woy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="week of year"} date to a [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of week"} date. Dec pads the left side of the [woy](#woy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="week of year"} and [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of week"} in dates with zeros so that we can distinguish between two-digit [woy](#woy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="weeks of year"} and three-digit [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of week"}. 

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup14}
$$\text{boydow} = (7 - \text{bow}\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod}7)\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod}7$$ {#eq-boydow}
:::

To find the [boy](#boy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of year"}[dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}, we first divide the [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of week"} by 7 and subtract the remainder from 7. Then, we divide the resulting difference by 7 and keep the remainder. We could also get the [boy](#boy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of year"}[dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} without a [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of week"} by turning the [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"} into a [doe](#doe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of era"} and then the [doe](#doe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of era"} into a [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}. Dec [woy](#woy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="week of year"} dates obfuscate🫣[pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} much more than [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of week"} dates, but may be useful for [week-based accounting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accounting_period#52%E2%80%9353-week_fiscal_year:~:text=used%20by%20companies%20that%20desire%20that%20their%20fiscal%20year%20always%20end%20on%20the%20same%20day%20of%20the%20week)🧾.

We can express any [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} as a half [domino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominoes#:~:text=a%20rectangular%20tile%2C%20usually%20with%20a%20line%20dividing%20its%20face%20into%20two%20square%20ends) in Dec [septenary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_numeral_systems#Standard_positional_numeral_systems:~:text=Septimal%2C-,septenary,-8) ([base7]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="septenary"}) and any [woy](#woy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="week of year"} as a [playing card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_52-card_deck#Terminology:~:text=52%20playing%20cards%3B-,13%20of%20each%20suit,-%3A%20clubs%2C%20diamonds%2C%20hearts) in Dec quadraquinquagesimal ([base54]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="quadraquinquagesimal"}) or a  Dec [quinary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quinary#:~:text=a%20numeral%20system%20with%20five%20as%20the%20base) ([base5]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="quinary"}) [playing card suit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playing_card_suit#:~:text=the%20categories%20into%20which%20the%20cards%20of%20a%20deck%20are%20divided) followed by a Dec [tridecimal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_numeral_systems#Standard_positional_numeral_systems:~:text=Tredecimal%2C-,tridecimal,-%5B40%5D) ([base13]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tridecimal"}) [constellation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecliptic#In_the_constellations:~:text=The%20ecliptic%20currently%20passes%20through%20the%20following%20thirteen%20constellations). The suit in a [base54]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="quadraquinquagesimal"} ([b54]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="quadraquinquagesimal"}) date: \${decYearColor6}[\${woyColor2}]{.playingcard}[\${dotwColor5}]{.halfdomino}, or a [base5]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="quinary"} ([b5]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="quinary"}) and [base13]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tridecimal"} ([b13]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tridecimal"}) date: 
\${decYearColor7}[\${woySuitColor}]{.playingcardsuit}[\${woySignColor}]{.zodiacsign}[\${dotwColor6}]{.halfdomino}, can be interpreted as a season.

:::::

Dec renders the Gregorian calendar [obsolete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obsolescence#:~:text=antiquated%2C%20out%20of%20date%2C%20old%2Dfashioned%2C%20no%20longer%20in%20general%20use%2C%20no%20longer%20useful%2C%20or%20superseded) with time units that supersede both months and weeks, but is also better than the Gregorian calendar at displaying a [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"} as a part of a date. Whereas Dec can expand [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"} into [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of week"}+[dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"}, [\${dotw0dotyColor}+\${dotwColor7}]{.nowrap}, the only standardized way to combine a [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}, [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"}, and month is to truncate an [RFC 7231](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7231#section-7.1.1.1:~:text=preferred%20format%20is-,Sun%2C%2006%20Nov,-1994%2008%3A49) date to 11 characters: \${loadStr}.

While [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of week"}+[dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"} are math expressions that evaluate to [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"}, RFC 7231 dates are character strings that include month and [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"} names which are abbreviated to 3 letters. Unlike names, the math notation underlying Dec dates is universal. In contrast to the [plus sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plus_and_minus_signs#:~:text=represents%20the%20operation%20of%20addition) in a Dec date, \${decYearColor8}+\${decDotyPadColor2}, the delimiters in a [RFC 9557](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9557/#name-optional-generation-and-ele:~:text=such%20as%3A%C2%B6-,2022%2D07%2D08T00,-%3A14%3A07%2B01) date are unrelated to math operators:  \${loadIso}.

# Day of month (dom) {#sec-dom}

Dec year+day dates can be expanded to display the "beginning of month" ([bom](#bom){#beginningofmonth .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"}) and [POSIX [dom]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"}](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/007904875/utilities/date.html#:~:text=day%20of%20the%20month%20as%20a%20decimal%20number%20%5B01%2C31%5D). The [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"} is the last [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} of the previous month because POSIX [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of month"} are one-based. We can think of the [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"} as [Dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of month"} 0 despite the fact that no such [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of month"} exists in POSIX or the Gregorian calendar. To obtain the [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"}, we can subtract the [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of month"} from the [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"}: \${monthNumberColor} = \${dotyInputColor7} -- \${dayofmonthColor}. 

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: boundsliders1
//| className: sliders
//| code-copy: false
Inputs.bind(Inputs.range([0, 364 + leapInput], {step: 1, label: "Day of year"}), viewof dotyInput)
Inputs.bind(Inputs.range([-365 - leapInput, -1], {step: 1, label: "Day of year"}), viewof dotyInput1)
```

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup15}
$$\text{bom} = \text{pid} - \text{dom}$$ {#eq-bom}
:::

We can find every possible [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"} using only a pair of hands🤲by counting index☝️and ring💍fingers as 30 days and other fingers as 31 days, as shown in the pair of images below. We start counting from -1, which is the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"} that preceeds the first "month of year" ([moy](#moy){#monthofyear .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="month of year"}): [Moy](#moy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="month of year"} [0]{.color0}. To cover 12 months with only 10 fingers, the first and last finger each represent 2 months.

:::{.hand}
![](/asset/left.svg){#lefthand}
![](/asset/right.svg){#righthand}
:::
[[Wikimedia](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Typing-colour_for-finger-positions.svg)]{.handlabel}

Like the [knuckle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knuckle_mnemonic#:~:text=a%20mnemonic%20device%20for%20remembering%20the%20number%20of%20days%20in%20the%20months%20of%20the%20Julian%20and%20Gregorian%20calendars)👊and [musical keyboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Month#:~:text=this%20cyclical%20pattern%20of%20month%20lengths%20matches%20the%20musical%20keyboard%20alternation%20of%20wide%20white%20keys%20(31%20days)%20and%20narrow%20black%20keys%20(30%20days))🎹[mnemonics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mnemonic#:~:text=any%20learning%20technique%20that%20aids%20information%20retention%20or%20retrieval%20in%20the%20human%20memory), the finger🖐counting technique described above is an attempt to make sense of the irregular pattern of [month lengths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Month#:~:text=Name-,Number,of%20days) in the Gregorian calendar️. We do not need mnemonics, [rhymes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty_Days_Hath_September), tables, [dactylonomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finger-counting#:~:text=counting%20using%20the%20fingers), or [mental calculations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mental_calculation#:~:text=arithmetical%20calculations%20made%20by%20the%20mind%2C%20within%20the%20brain%2C%20with%20no%20help%20from%20any%20supplies) to use [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"} or [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of ten days"}, because all of the required information is plainly visible in the [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"}.

To convert a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} to or from a [POSIX month](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/007904875/utilities/date.html#:~:text=Month%20as%20a%20decimal%20number%20%5B01%2C12%5D) and [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"}, we can use parts of the [`civil_from_days`](https://howardhinnant.github.io/date_algorithms.html#civil_from_days){.mono .under} and [`days_from_civil`](https://howardhinnant.github.io/date_algorithms.html#days_from_civil){.mono .under} algorithms [@hinnant2021date]. POSIX months are one-based and start at [Moy](#moy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="month of year"} [10]{.color306by365}, whereas [moy](#moy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="months of year"} are zero-based and thus begin from [Moy](#moy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="month of year"} [0]{.color0}. To obtain a [moy](#moy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="month of year"}, we can plug a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} into @eq-pid2moy or a POSIX month into @eq-month2moy.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup16}
$$\text{moy} = \left\lfloor\dfrac{\text{pid} \ast 5 + 2}{153}\right\rfloor$$ {#eq-pid2moy}

$$\text{month} = (\text{moy} + 3) \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod} 12$$ {#eq-moy2month}

$$\text{bom} = \left\lfloor\dfrac{\text{moy} \ast 153 + 2}{5}\right\rfloor - \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{[}\text{UTC offset} \ge 0\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{]}$$ {#eq-moy2bom}

$$\text{dom} = \text{pid} - \text{bom}$$ {#eq-dom}

$$\text{moy} = (\text{month} + 9) \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod} 12$$ {#eq-month2moy}

$$\text{pid} = \text{bom} + \text{dom}$$ {#eq-bomdomsum}
:::

POSIX months and [moy](#moy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="months of year"} are shifted in relation to each other because the Dec epoch, [0000]{.color0}+[000]{.color0}, is 2 months later than the Gregorian calendar epoch: [-0001]{.color99by100}+[306]{.color306by365}. To convert years, we add 1 to the [yoe]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"} or subtract 1 from the Gregorian calendar️ "common era year" ([cey](#cey){#commonerayear .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="common era year"}) if the [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} is greater than [305]{.color305by365}, the [moy](#moy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="month of year"} is greater than [9]{.color275by365}, or the POSIX month is less than [3]{.color0}.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup17}
$$
\text{cey}=\text{yoe}+\begin{cases}
  1&{\begin{aligned}
    &\text{ if } \text{pid} \,\ \ \ \ \ \gt 305\\
    &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction}{\lor}\text{moy}\ \ \ \ \gt 9\\
    &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction}{\lor}\text{month}\lt 3\end{aligned}}\\\\
  0&{\text{ otherwise}}\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-cey}
:::

A similar adjustment is needed when dealing with negative UTC offsets. Dec does not permit "time zone offsets" ([tzo](#tzo){#timezoneoffset .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"}) to be negative and therefore adds one day to every negative [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"}. @eq-moy2bom takes into account the possibility of a negative UTC offset and adjusts the [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"} accordingly. Starting from zero, we can count every adjusted [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"} on our fingers.

:::{.hand}
![](/asset/leftnegtzo.svg){#lefthand}
![](/asset/rightnegtzo.svg){#righthand}
:::
[[Wikimedia](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Typing-colour_for-finger-positions.svg)]{.handlabel}

The adjusted [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of month"} in the images above are exactly the same as the values in the rightmost column of the first table under the heading "[Computing day-of-year from month and day-of-month](https://howardhinnant.github.io/date_algorithms.html#Computing%20day-of-year%20from%20month%20and%20day-of-month)" in [[`chrono`]{.mono .under}-Compatible Low-Level Date Algorithms](https://howardhinnant.github.io/date_algorithms.html) [@hinnant2021date]. The adjusted and unadjusted [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of month"} can be generated using @eq-moy2bom whenever necessary.

Dec dates can also be explained in terms of [object oriented programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object-oriented_programming#:~:text=a%20programming%20paradigm%20based%20on%20objects). In this analogy, an object is a blueprint for Dec dates and an [instance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instance_(computer_science)#:~:text=a%20specific%20occurrence%20of%20a%20software%20element%20that%20is%20based%20on%20a%20type%20definition) represents a specific Dec date. When we create an instance, we can specify the date that it will represent by providing either a [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"} and [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"} for it to store or a [cey](#cey){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="common era year"}, month, and [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"} for it to transform into a [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"} and [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"}.

Regardless of the input, only a [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"} and [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"} are stored as [instance attributes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instance_variable#:~:text=each%20instantiated%20object%20of%20the%20class%20has%20a%20separate%20copy). Our instance must contain one instance method for every potential output that is not an instance attribute. Instance methods can use instance attributes to produce their output. For example, a method based on Equations -@eq-pid2moy, -@eq-moy2month, -@eq-moy2bom, and -@eq-dom could turn a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"} into a month and [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"}.

@fig-conv below visualizes how an instance that represents the UNIX epoch would convert its [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"} and [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"} into a [cey](#cey){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="common era year"}, month, [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"}, and [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}. For simplicity, @fig-conv omits the [coe](#coe){.under .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="cycle of era"}, [yoc](#yoc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of cycle"}, and [doc](#doc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of cycle"} needed to convert a Dec date into a [doe](#doe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of era"}, the [moy](#moy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="months of year"} and [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"} required to split a [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} into a month and a [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"}, and the negative UTC offset adjustment for [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of month"} and [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"}.
