Even though a month is about as long as a [lunation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_month#Synodic_month:~:text=the%20average%20period%20of%20the%20Moon%27s%20orbit%20with%20respect%20to%20the%20line%20joining%20the%20Sun%20and%20Earth) and a week is almost as long as one of the four major [lunar phases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_phase#:~:text=the%20new%20moon%2C%20the%20first%20quarter%2C%20the%20full%20moon%2C%20and%20the%20last%20quarter), Gregorian calendar months, [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of month"}, weeks, and [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"} do not provide any information about the level of illumination of the Moon🌙by the Sun☀️. To be fair, Gregorian calendar months can provide the season, albeit not as directly as [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"}, [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of ten days"}, or [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"}.

# Day of bimester (dob) {#sec-dob}

We can get a sense of how much of the surface of the Moon is illuminated by expanding a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} in a Dec date into a "beginning of bimester" ([bob](#bob){#beginningofbimester .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of bimester"}) and "day of bimester" ([dob](#dob){#dayofbimester .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"}) in place of a [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"} and [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"} or a [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of week"} and [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"}. A Dec bimester is exactly 59 days and is roughly a tenth of a percent shorter than two lunations: 59 / (29.53 * 2) * 100% &asymp; 99.9%.

To obtain a [dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"}, Dec employs an algorithm based on the [`from_days`](https://github.com/HowardHinnant/date/blob/7875f43aa9288d176191c83e8284d61acdd5ab7c/include/date/islamic.h#L2252) [method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Method_%28computer_programming%29#:~:text=a%20procedure%20associated%20with%20an%20object) of the `year_month_day` [object](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object_(computer_science)#:~:text=a%20semantic%20entity%20that%20has%20state%2C%20behavior%2C%20and%20identity) in the [`islamic.h`](https://github.com/HowardHinnant/date/blob/master/include/date/islamic.h) file of the [`date`](https://github.com/HowardHinnant/date) [repository](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repository_%28version_control%29#:~:text=a%20data%20structure%20that%20stores%20metadata%20for%20a%20set%20of%20files%20or%20directory%20structure) by [Howard Hinnant](https://howardhinnant.github.io) -@hinnant2021date. Equations -@eq-dot, -@eq-yot, and -@eq-dob produces a "day of tricennium" ([dot](#dot){#dayoftricennium .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of tricennium"}) and a "year of tricennium" ([yot](#yot){#yearoftricennium .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of tricennium"}) along the way to turning a [doe](#doe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of era"} into a [dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"}. A Dec [tricennium](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/tricennium#:~:text=A%20period%20of%20thirty%20years) is 10631 days.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup18}
$$
\text{dot} = (\text{doe} + 3124) \bmod 10631
$$ {#eq-dot}

$$
\text{yot} = \left\lfloor\frac{30\ast\text{doc}+10646}{10631}\right\rfloor - 1
$$ {#eq-yot}

$$
\text{dob} = \left(\text{dot} - \left(354\ast\text{yot} + \left\lfloor \frac{11\ast(\text{yot}+1)+3}{30} \right\rfloor \right) \right) \bmod 59
$$ {#eq-dob}
:::

:::{.panel-tabset group="language"}
### Julia

```{julia}
function dob(doe)
    dot = mod(doe + 3124, 10631)
    yot = floor(Int, (30 * dot + 10646) / 10631) - 1
    return mod(
        dot - (yot * 354 + floor(
            Int, (11 * (yot + 1) + 3) / 30)), 59)
end
dob(227320)
```

### Observable JavaScript

```{ojs}
function dob(doe) {
  const dot = (doe + 3124) % 10631;
  const yot = Math.floor((30 * dot + 10646) / 10631) - 1;
  return (
    dot - (yot * 354 + Math.floor((
      11 * (yot + 1) + 3) / 30))) % 59;
}
dob(227320)
```

### Python

```{python}
def dob(doe):
    dot = (doe + 3124) % 10631
    yot = (30 * dot + 10646) // 10631 - 1
    return (
        dot - (yot * 354 + (
            11 * (yot + 1) + 3) // 30)) % 59
dob(227320)
```

### R

```{r}
dob <- function(doe) {
  dot <- (doe + 3124) %% 10631
  yot <- floor((30 * dot + 10646) / 10631) - 1
  (dot - (yot * 354 + floor((
    11 * (yot + 1) + 3) / 30))) %% 59
}
dob(227320)
```

:::

A tricennium can be evenly split into 19 lunar common years and 11 lunar leap years, 180 bimesters and 11 lunar leap days, or 169 lunar short months and 191 lunar long months: 19 &times; 354 + 11 &times; 355 = 180 &times; 59 + 11 = 169 &times; 29 + 191 &times; 30 = 10631. Likewise, we can evenly divide a bimester into 1 lunar long month and 1 lunar short month: 30 + 29 = 59.

We can learn that the current bimester began \${decDobColor} days ago on Day [\${decBobSign1}]{.mono}${decBobColor} by looking at the current year+[bob](#bob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of bimester"}+[dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"} Dec date: \${decYearColor9}[\${decBobSign}]{.mono}\${decBobColor1}[+]{.mono}\${decDobColor1}. All bimesters begin with [Dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"} [0]{.color0} and end with [Dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"} [58]{.color58by59}. After 12 or 18 bimesters, a lunar leap day occurs. Dec designates lunar leap days as [Dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of bimester"} [[0]{.grave}]{.color0}, which is similar to how solar leap days appear when expressed as [[mi]{.overline}[d]{.grave}](#mid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="next mixed integer days of year"}.

Given that a bimester is slightly shorter than two lunations, we expect lunar phases and [dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"} to slowly drift apart over 2 or 3 lunar years before being put back into alignment by [Dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"} [[0]{.grave}]{.color0}, but we should generally observe a new🌑moon on [Dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"} [0]{.color0} and [29]{.color29by59}, first quarter🌓moon on [Dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"} [7]{.color07by59} and [37]{.color37by59}, full🌕moon on [Dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"} [14]{.color14by59} and [44]{.color44by59}, and last quarter🌗moon on [Dob]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"} [22]{.color22by59} and [52]{.color52by59}.

Each moon diagram in the [small multiple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_multiple#:~:text=a%20series%20of%20similar%20graphs%20or%20charts%20using%20the%20same%20scale%20and%20axes) grid below has a [dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of bimester"} above it. When the "Layout" radio input beneath the grid is set to "Dec", the grid itself portrays a lunar year, its rows depict lunar months, its row labels are zero-based lunar [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"}, and each of its columns has moon diagrams that are in the same lunar phase and [dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of bimester"} which have the same last digit.

When we instead set the "Layout" radio input to "Gregorian", the grid itself represents a Gregorian calendar year, its rows stand for Gregorian calendar months, its row labels are zero-based Gregorian calendar [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"}, and its columns group days by [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}. Use the "Year" [number input](https://github.com/observablehq/inputs/blob/main/README.md#inputsnumberextent-options) to see how the lunation patterns of the two layouts change over time.

:::{#moonobservable}
{{< include /dec/date/_moon.qmd >}}
:::

Unsurprisingly, the "Dec" layout is almost indistinguishable every lunar year and the "Gregorian" layout varies wildly across Gregorian calendar years. To be fair, we would also see wild variation in the lunation pattern of Dec solar years, because [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"} and [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of ten days"}, like Gregorian calendar months, closely follow the seasons and thus are entirely out of step with the lunar phases.

Dec dates in the year+[bob](#bob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of bimester"}+[dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"} format allow us to track the lunar phases and then sum the [bob](#bob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of bimester"} and [dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"} to identify dates using pid, identify seasons using h, gauge progress through the seasons using doh, or classify days as work or rest days using dox. Just as we can split a solar year in 73 [p](#p){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentadays"}, we can also divide a bimester into 12 "pentadays of bimester" ([pob](#pob){#pentadayofbimester .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentadays of bimester"}).

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup19}
$$\text{pob} = \left\lfloor\dfrac{\text{dob}}{5}\right\rfloor$$ {#eq-pob}
:::

In general, the moon goes from new moon to waxing crescent in [Pob](#pob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Pentaday of bimester"} [0]{.color0} and [6]{.color30by59}, from waxing crescent to waxing gibbous in [Pob](#pob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Pentaday of bimester"} [1]{.color05by59} and [7]{.color35by59}, from waxing gibbous to full moon in [Pob](#pob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Pentaday of bimester"} [2]{.color10by59} and [8]{.color40by59}, from full moon to waning gibbous in [Pob](#pob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Pentaday of bimester"} [3]{.color15by59} and [9]{.color45by59}, from waning gibbous to waning crescent in [Pob](#pob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Pentaday of bimester"} [4]{.color20by59} and [10]{.color50by59}, and finally from waning crescent to new moon in [Pob](#pob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Pentaday of bimester"} [5]{.color25by59} and [11]{.color55by59}.

The first quarter moon occurs around the middle of [Pob](#pob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Pentaday of bimester"} [1]{.color05by59} and [7]{.color35by59}, while the last quarter moon appears near the center of [Pob](#pob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Pentaday of bimester"} [4]{.color20by59} and [10]{.color50by59}. Solar common years, lunar leap years, lunar long months, and [x]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of ten days"} can be divided evenly into [p](#p){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentadays"}. Solar leap years, lunar common years, lunar short months, and bimesters are all only 1 day off from being evenly divisible by 5.

Dec lunar years and months are based on the [Lunar Hijri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_calendar#:~:text=a%20lunar%20calendar%20consisting%20of%2012%20lunar%20months%20in%20a%20year%20of%20354%20or%20355%20days) calendar. Whereas Lunar Hijri calendar dates consist of lunar years, months, and [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of month"}, the analogous Dec dates comprise solar years, [bob](#bob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of bimester"}, and [dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of bimester"}. An advantage of solar years is that it is easier to calculate the [syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"} via Equations -@eq-leap and -@eq-leap2syl than the "lunar year length" ([lyl](#lyl){#lunaryearlength .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="lunar year length"}) with Equations -@eq-lunarleap and -@eq-leap2lyl below.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup20}
$$
\text{lunarleap}=\begin{cases}
  1&{\begin{aligned}
    &\text{ if } \text{yot} = 1\\
    &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction}{\lor}\text{yot} = 4\\
    &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction}{\lor}\text{yot} = 6\\
    &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction}{\lor}\text{yot} = 9\\
    &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction}{\lor}\text{yot} = 12\\
    &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction}{\lor}\text{yot} = 15\\
    &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction}{\lor}\text{yot} = 17\\
    &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction}{\lor}\text{yot} = 20\\
    &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction}{\lor}\text{yot} = 23\\
    &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction}{\lor}\text{yot} = 25\\
    &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction}{\lor}\text{yot} = 28\end{aligned}}\\\\
  0&{\text{ otherwise}}\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-lunarleap}

$$\text{lyl} = 354 + \text{lunarleap}$$ {#eq-leap2lyl}
:::

To find the [lyl](#lyl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="lunar year length"}, we compare the [yot](#yot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of tricennium"} against 10 values. To find the length of a Gregorian calendar month, we use an index to [choose from 12 values](https://howardhinnant.github.io/date_algorithms.html#last_day_of_month_common_year). In contrast, lunar months follow a simple pattern. According to @eq-lunarmonth below, lunar month indexes are one-based, even-numbered lunar months have 29 days, and odd-numbered lunar months have 30 days. 

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup21}
$$
\text{lunarmonth} = \left\lfloor\dfrac{11\ast\left(\text{dot} - 354\ast\text{yot} - \left\lfloor\dfrac{11\ast(\text{yot}+1)+3}{30}\right\rfloor\right) + 330}{325}\right\rfloor
$$ {#eq-lunarmonth}
:::

# Moon {#moon}

“The sky is the limit” is an understatement, because Decalendar can be adapted for people living on the Moon and other celestial bodies. Rather than days, lunar inhabitants would be best served by "spin orbit intervals" ([soi](#soi){#spinorbitinterval .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit intervals"}), which are the inverse of the difference in the [sidereal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidereal#:~:text=Sidereal%2C%20meaning%20%22-,of%20the%20stars,-%22%2C%20may%20refer%20to) frequencies of a [spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth%27s_rotation#:~:text=the%20rotation%20of%20planet%20Earth%20around%20its%20own%20axis) of the Earth on its axis and an [orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbit_of_the_Moon#:~:text=the%20Sun.%20It-,orbits%20Earth,-in%20the%20prograde) of the Moon around the Earth.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup22}
$$
\dfrac{1}{1\div\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#:~:text=4.09%20seconds%28%2C%20or-,0.99726968,-of%20a%20solar}{0.99726968}-1\div\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_month#:~:text=stars%20%28Latin:%20sidera%29:-,27.321661,-days%20%2827%20d%29}{27.321661}} = 1.03505
$$ {#eq-soi}
:::

The number of [soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit intervals"} per mean [tropical year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_year#:~:text=the%20time%20that%20the%20Sun%20takes%20to%20return%20to%20the%20same%20position%20in%20the%20sky) is [365.2421897](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_year#:~:text=1%2C%202000%2C%20was-,365.2421897,-or%20365%C2%A0ephemeris) &div; 1.03505 = 352.87395749. We can match this quite closely by setting the lunar Decalendar (Decalunar) [syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"} to 352 [soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit intervals"} if the year is evenly divisible by 8 and to 353 [soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit intervals"}, otherwise: 7 &div; 8 -- 0.87395749 = 0.00104251 &asymp; 1 &div; 959. For greater precision, the Decalunar [syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"} could be calculated as in @eq-lunarsyl. 

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup23}
$$
353 - \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{[}\text{y} \bmod 8 = 0 \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction}{\lor} \text{y} \bmod 959 = 479
\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{]}
$$ {#eq-lunarsyl}
:::

The Decalunar epoch should be a new moon that occurs close to midnight on [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[0]{.color0} so that the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} and the "[soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit interval"} of year" ([soy](#soy){#soiofyear .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="soi of year"}) would have a common origin and thus be easier to compare. As the initial lunar epoch, I would choose the [boy](#boy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of year"} [1976]{.color76by100}, the year of the [last lunar probe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_lunar_probes#:~:text=Lunar%20exploration%20%281959%E2%80%93-,1976,-%29) of the [Space Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Race#:~:text=a%2020th%2Dcentury%20competition%20between%20the%20Cold%20War%20rivals%2C%20the%20United%20States%20and%20the%20Soviet%20Union%2C%20to%20achieve%20superior%20spaceflight%20capability), but a later epoch should be chosen once the Moon is permanently inhabited.

In Decalunar, a lunar leap year is 343 [soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit intervals"} instead of 355 days, a lunar common year is 342 [soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit intervals"} rather than 354 days, a bimester is 57 [soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit intervals"} in lieu of 59 days, a short month is 28 [soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit intervals"} as opposed to 29 days, and a long month is 29 [soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit intervals"} instead of 30 days, and lunations are monitored by expanding a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} into a [bob](#bob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of bimester"} and "[soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit interval"} of bimester" ([sob](#sob){#soiofbimester .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="soi of bimester"}) rather than a [bob](#bob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of bimester"} and [dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"}.

A Decalunar lunar common year can be split evenly into 6 bimesters or 3 quadrimesters: 342 = 6 &times; 57 = 3 &times; 114. Decalendar and Decalunar can follow the same lunar leap year pattern because the fractional part of 12 [synodic months](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_month#Synodic_month:~:text=the%20average%20period%20of%20the%20Moon%27s%20orbit%20with%20respect%20to%20the%20line%20joining%20the%20Sun%20and%20Earth) is nearly identical for days and [soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit intervals"}: [29.53059](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_month#Synodic_month:~:text=synodic%20month%29%20is-,29.53059%20days,-or%2029%20d) &times; 12 [mod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder) 1 &asymp; 354.367 [mod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder) 1 &asymp; 354.367 &div; 1.03505 [mod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder) 1 &asymp; 342.367 [mod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder) 1.

Both Decalendar and Decalunar rely on the [syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"} for precise timekeeping over long periods, and thus can adapt whenever the [lyl](#lyl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="lunar year length"} diverges from observed lunations. If need be, we can move a day or two between the [bob](#bob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of bimester"} and [dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"} or a [soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit intervals"} or two between the [bob](#bob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of bimester"} and [sob](#sob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="soi of bimester"} to better match lunar observations without affecting the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} or [soy](#soy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="soi of year"} as per Equations -@eq-sob and -@eq-bobplusdob.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup24}
$$
\text{soy} = \text{bob}_{\text{s}} + \text{sob}
$$ {#eq-sob}

$$
\text{doy} = \text{bob}_{\text{d}} + \text{dob}
$$ {#eq-bobplusdob}
:::

# Mars {#mars}

Serependitiously, Earth and Mars rotate on their respective axes almost at the same rate. A Martian [sol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_sol#:~:text=for%20sun%29%20is-,a%20solar%20day%20on%20Mars,-%3B%20that%20is%2C%20a) is [1.02749125](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_sol#:~:text=1.02749125%20Earth%20days), which is about 0.76% of a day less than a [soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit interval"}. The Martian variant of Decalendar is called Dec[arean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_adjectivals_and_demonyms_of_astronomical_bodies#Planets:~:text=Martian%2C%20Martial%2C-,Arean,-%5B9%5D) after [Ares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ares#:~:text=Greek%20god%20of%20war%20and%20courage), one of the twelve Olympians and the god of war in Greek mythology. Decarean leap years are determined by cycles of 22 years or 14709 sols.

In a Decarean cycle, there are 9 short years with 668 sols and 13 long years with 669 sols. Years that are not evenly divisible by 2 always have 669 sols, which is easy to remember because odd years have an odd number of sols. There are also 2 even years with 669 sols every cycle which are always 10 years apart within a cycle and 12 years apart between cycles.

The Decarean epoch is 1953+084.41516515, matches the currently used system for [numbering Martian years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timekeeping_on_Mars#Year_numbering:~:text=beginning%20May%2024%2C%201953), has the same fractional part as the [Mars Sol Date epoch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timekeeping_on_Mars#Mars_Sol_Date:~:text=a%20running%20count%20of%20sols%20since%2029%20December%201873), and coincides with the Martian [northward equinox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timekeeping_on_Mars#Definition_of_year_and_seasons:~:text=0-,northward%20equinox,-1%2C%202%2C%203), but is otherwise [arbitrary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timekeeping_on_Mars#Year_numbering:~:text=the%20choice%20as-,%22arbitrary%22,-%2C%20the%20great%20dust). I first designed Decarean with [Martian colonization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonization_of_Mars#:~:text=establishing%20permanent%20human%20settlements%20on%20the%20planet%20Mars) in mind, but now I believe humanity should concentrate on [robotic spaceflight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceflight#Uncrewed:~:text=without%20people%20on%20board).

As our technology improves, the cost of sending robots into space will decrease and the return on investments into robotic missions will increase. In contrast, [human spaceflight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_spaceflight#:~:text=spaceflight%20with%20a%20crew%20or%20passengers%20aboard%20a%20spacecraft) will remain expensive and limited by human anatomy and physiology. More importantly, robots are much less likely than astronauts to [contaminate Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interplanetary_contamination#:~:text=It%20is%20thought%20that%20many,may%20have%20already%20been%20contaminated.) with biological material from Earth.

We need to avoid contamination so as not to complicate the search for [extraterrestrial life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extraterrestrial_life#:~:text=life%20that%20originates%20from%20another%20world%20rather%20than%20on%20Earth) or traces thereof on Mars. Natural resources should only be collected from Martian sites that can be confirmed to never have harbored extraterrestrial life. We should first focus exclusively on exploration, then can begin exploitation, but should refrain from colonization of Mars.

# Venus {#venus}

Even if we can prove without a doubt that Mars is and always has been devoid of extraterrestrial life, we still should not invest resources into enabling Mars to support human inhabitants, because those resources are much better spent on [terraforming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terraforming_of_Venus#:~:text=transform%20Venus%20from%20a%20planet%20hostile%20to%20life%20to%20one%20that%20could%20sustainably%20host%20humans) and then [colonizing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonization_of_Venus#:~:text=establishing%20human%20settlements%20on%20the%20planet%20Venus) Venus, the planet that is [most similar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus#:~:text=similar%20to%20Earth%20in%20size%20and%20mass%20and%20is%20often%20described%20as%20Earth%27s%20%22sister%22%20or%20%22twin%22) to Earth in size, mass, composition, and orbit.

Whereas Venus should be the focal point for colonization, the Moon and its L1 and L2 [Lagrange points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrange_point#:~:text=points%20of%20equilibrium%20for%20small%2Dmass%20objects%20under%20the%20gravitational%20influence%20of%20two%20massive%20orbiting%20bodies) will form the central hub for spaceflight. The proximity of the Moon allows for efficient communication with Earth. At light speed, radio signals can travel from Earth to the Moon in 1.25 to 1.39 Dec seconds ([s](#s){#second .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"}), Venus in 132 to 907 [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec second"}, or Mars in 190 to 1390 [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec second"}.

To put these numbers in context, the speed of light is around 7.195 [taurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn_(angle)#Tau_proposals:~:text=%E2%81%A0%20turn-,Circumference%20of%20a%20circle,-%F0%9D%90%B6) ([c](#c){#taur .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taurs"}) per [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"}, the [Equator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equator#:~:text=the%20circle%20of%20latitude%20that%20divides%20Earth%20into%20the%20Northern%20and%20Southern%20Hemispheres) is about 1 [c](#c){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taurs"}, there are exactly 90000 [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"} or 86400 [International System of Units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_System_of_Units#:~:text=the%20world%27s%20most%20widely%20used%20system%20of%20measurement) ([SI](#si){#internationalsystemofunits .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="International System of Units"}) seconds in 1 day, and the approximate distance from Earth ranges from 9 to 10 [c](#c){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taurs"} for the Moon, 950 to 6525 [c](#c){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taurs"} for Venus, 1365 to 10000 [c](#c){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taurs"} for Mars, and 14700 to 24200 [c](#c){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taurs"} for Jupiter.

Mars represents the outer boundary of both the [habitable zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habitable_zone#:~:text=the%20range%20of%20orbits%20around%20a%20star%20within%20which%20a%20planetary%20surface%20could%20potentially%20support%20liquid%20water) and the [terrestrial planets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrestrial_planet#:~:text=a%20class%20of%20planet%20that%20is%20composed%20primarily%20of%20silicate%2C%20rocks%2C%20or%20metals) in our [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System#:~:text=the%20gravitationally%20bound%20system%20of%20the%20Sun%20and%20the%20masses%20that%20orbit%20it). The nearest possibly habitable  [exoplanet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exoplanet#:~:text=a%20planet%20outside%20the%20Solar%20System), [Proxima Centauri b](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proxima_Centauri_b#:~:text=an%20exoplanet%20orbiting%20within%20the%20habitable%20zone%20of%20the%20red%20dwarf%20star%20Proxima%20Centauri%20in%20the%20constellation%20Centaurus),  is roughly 1 billion (10^9^) [c](#c){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taurs"} away. The pool of nearby [potentially habitable exoplanets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_potentially_habitable_exoplanets#Main_list:~:text=a%20list%20of%20confirmed%20exoplanets%20within%20the%20circumstellar%20habitable%20zone%20that%20are%20either%20under%2010%20Earth%20masses%20or%20smaller%20than%202.5%20Earth%20radii%20and%20thus%20have%20a%20chance%20of%20being%20rocky) may expand in the future, perhaps due to the [Big Crunch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Crunch#:~:text=the%20expansion%20of%20the%20universe%20eventually%20reverses%20and%20the%20universe%20recollapses) or a [galaxy merger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_merger#:~:text=when%20two%20%28or%20more%29%20galaxies%20collide) involving the [Milky Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milky_Way#:~:text=the%20galaxy%20that%20includes%20the%20Solar%20System).

While we study potentially habitable exoplanets, we can create a habitable planet in our own backyard by terraforming Venus. To speed up the process, many terraformation approaches can be pursued in parallel. [Flybys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flyby_(spaceflight)#:~:text=a%20spaceflight%20operation%20in%20which%20a%20spacecraft%20passes%20near%20another%20body) of asteroids or comets could increase the [rotational speed of Venus and expand its orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terraforming_of_Venus#cite_note-45:~:text=move%20a%20planet%20in%20its%20orbit%2C%20or%20increase%20the%20speed%20of%20rotation) to bring it into the habitable zone and closer to Earth. 

An expanded orbit would cool Venus and a faster rotational speed might promote the development of a protective [magnetosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetosphere#:~:text=a%20region%20of%20space%20surrounding%20an%20astronomical%20object%2C%20such%20as%20a%20planet%20or%20other%20object%2C%20in%20which%20charged%20particles%20are%20affected%20by%20that%20object%27s%20magnetic%20field). Venus has an [axial tilt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axial_tilt#:~:text=the%20angle%20between%20an%20object%27s%20rotational%20axis%20and%20its%20orbital%20axis) that is just 7.4 [milliturns]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousandths of a turn"} short of a half turn and thus has no seasons. Therefore, the [Venusian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_adjectivals_and_demonyms_of_astronomical_bodies#Planets:~:text=%5B7%5D-,Venusian,-%2C%20Cytherean) Decalendar (De[cyther](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_adjectivals_and_demonyms_of_astronomical_bodies#Planets:~:text=Venusian%2C-,Cytherean,-cythero%2D)) does not need to count its own solar years and can instead use the same [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"} as Decalendar.

On Venus, a solar year is 224.7 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} and a solar day is 116.75 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"}. Decyther could match Venusian solar days exceptionally well with cycles of 4 years or 1401 days that comprise 3 short years of 350 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} and 1 long year of 351 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"}. Each Decyther year consists of 6 bimesters. Each Decyther bimester is 58 + [\[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise){.nounder}*i* [mod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder) 8 ∈ {0, 3, 6}[\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise){.nounder} [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} long, where *i* is the zero-based bimester index. 

A Decyther bimester represents half of a Venusian solar day and is thus analogous to half of a day on Earth or half of a lunation on the Moon, even though 1 bimester lasts about as long as 2 lunations. At Venusian midnight, the [ante meridiem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/12-hour_clock#:~:text=%2C%20translating%20to%20%22-,before%20midday,-%22%29%20and%20p.m) bimester of a new solar day begins immediately after the [post meridiem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/12-hour_clock#:~:text=%2C%20translating%20to%20%22-,after%20midday,-%22%29.%5B1) bimester of the preceding solar day ends.

Likewise, Venusian noon marks the start of the post meridiem bimester and the end of the ante meridiem bimester. In Decyther, Venusian midnight and Venusian noon are both denoted by [Dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"} [0]{.color0}. When we combine an ante meridiem bimester with the post meridiem bimester that follows it, we get a Decyther [quadrimester](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/quadrimester#:~:text=A%20period%20of%20four%20months%20or%20about%20four%20months) which can be either 116 or 117 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} long.

Like Decalendar, Decyther identifies bimesters using [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="years of era"} and [bob](#bob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of bimester"}. Decyther uses the same [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"} and [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} as Decalendar, but expands [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"} into [bob](#bob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of bimester"} and [dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of bimester"} to monitor Venusian solar days instead of lunations. Decyther uses bimesters in spite of that fact that Venus does not have a moon. Despite the fact that Mars has two moons, Decarean has no need for bimesters.

Venus and Mars often appear to be dissimilar to Earth in completely opposite ways and it seems that when one is similar to Earth, the other is not. For example, the axial tilts of Earth, Mars, and Venus are 6.5, 7, and 49.25 [centiturns]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hundredths of a turn"}, respectively. The unique characteristics of these three planets present an opportunity to showcase the versatility of Decalendar.

# Summary {.unnumbered #tldr}

At its heart❤️, Decalendar is a simple system that measures time solely in integer years and days. A Dec [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"}+[pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} date is essentially an abbreviation of [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"}+[pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"}/[syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"}, which is a math expression that sums the [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"} with the fraction of the year that has elapsed. The difference between the denominator and the numerator of this fraction is the number of days left in the year.

Dec can expand a date to display different kinds of information without changing the decimal year value that the date represents. Date expansion allows Decalendar to use measurement units other than years and days, such as bimesters, months, and weeks. In essence, expanded dates show the number of days since or until a reference point, such as a [bob](#bob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of bimester"}, [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of month"}, or [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of week"}.

Regardless of the number of days per month, we can describe a [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"} as a month in numeric form and a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} as the sum of a [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"} and [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"}. By expanding [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"} into [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of week"} and [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"}, Decalendar provides unmatched support for weekly schedules. Thanks to date expansion, Decalendar is truly unrivaled and can be referred to as ***the*** calendar or the one calendar [to rule them all](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Ring#:~:text=One%20ring%20to%20rule%20them%20all)!
